Let me, then, recommend to you the stirring and horse-hoeing of your root-plants during dry weather, if you wish to secure the greatest development for them which is attainable under such circumstances. Let me now proceed gentlemen, to point out to you one the or two first things connected with draining In the place, you will observe that, if it be fact,

as I have stated, that the more porous a soil is, the greater amount of surface it exposes, and the greater amount of substance it absorbs from the air, when the pores of the soil are filled with water, the soil cannot be taking anything from the air. It is, therefore clearly the very first principle of good practical farming not to have an excess of moisture in the land. The next point has reference to the depth of drains. Now 1 don't know whether all you gentlemen are aware that there is a certain principle in nature but It is a long term j called capillary attraction. it means the attraction of tubeB or fissures. If I had this jar (pointing to a large glass jar) nearly full of common garden soil, and if 1 of were penetrate the bottom the to allow water to jar, I should find the water rising up gradually until it got perhaps to the very top of the vessel. It would rise by what is called capillary attraction. Again, if I were to put a piece of sugar into half a tea spoonful of water, the sugar would drain up all the water by capillary attraction. A similar effect i# produced in the case of the soil. When the water got to the top, it would be evaporated. When water evaporates, it produces cold. You are all aware of that, from your own experience. If you get wet through, you catch cold, from that cause. The evaporation of excess-water from the surface of soils, therefore, cools them below the natural temperature, and retards the growth of plants accordingly. It is, therefore, neces-

sary that you should keep this point, towards which water rises by capillary attraction, eighteen inches or two feet below the upper surface of the soil ; for if you do not do that, you will have the moisture mounting nearly to the surface, and the cold arising from its evaporation there will produce pernicious effects. It cannot be necessary for me to tell you how essential it is that the roots of plants should be kept warm. Yet all know that in hothouses, and places used for forcing plants, great importance is attached to bottom heat One of the great points, therefore, which I have to impress upon you, with respect to draining, is the absolute necessity of so managing the operation as to prevent that evaporation at the surface, which caunot hut produce a most injurious effect upon the plant Let us next observe that there is, I tnink, considerable misunderstanding gene ally prevailing as to the manner in which drains act. We are all apt to imagine that, when we have put drains into the soil, they act from the surface, and that the water flows into them from above, and passes away. Now, g ntlemen, the water never flows into the drains from the surface ; it sinks through the land, and rises to the bottom of the drain. I recollect, some time ago, finding some of my agricultural friends further ea6t very much puzzled in relerence to a particular case of drainage. THE MUTINY IN INDIA. The following despatch has been received by the Foreign Otiice : þÿ (By Electric Telegraph.) From Vice-Consul Raven, dated Trieste, Wednesday, August 12th, noon þÿ Received 5-26 p.m. Subjoined is a message to Sir James Melville, Loudon, forwarded by me from Captain Johnson, Alexandria, under date from Alexandria, August 7th. The Indian mail uas arrived, with news from Bombay to July 14th. Delhi had not fallen up to the 27th of June. There had been a good deal of fighting outside the fort walls. The rebels were repulsed with loss on every occasion. General Van Cortlandt, when marching upon Sirsa and Hissar, had two engagements with the rebels near Sirsa, the last being a very decided one. The rebels fled in disorder, leaving 200 dead on the field, besides prisoners. The Punjaub remains quiet. General Woodbum's column crushed the rebellion at Aurungabad. Intelligence has been received of the mutiny of the troops at Moradabad, Fyzabad Seetapore, Agoro, Nowgaon, Baudai Futtyghur, Mhow, and Indore. Tne Governors of the Presidencies are at their respective seats. The first batch of China troops (the 5th Fusiliers) arrived in Calcutta per Simoom, about the 2nd of July.

By another telegraphic despatch we are informed that the Bombay and Madras armies continue firmly loyal. Delhi was reported to be full of sick and wounded, and the cholera was prevalent. Reinforcements had begun to reach the British camp before that city. Our force before Delhi is stated to be from 7000 to 8000 Europeans and 5000 natives.

CHINA. IIong Kong, June 24. Nothing importance has occurred here of since the last mail. Lord Elgin has not arrived. The 5th and 90th Regiments are to be diverted to India. The Chinese report that the Emperor has abdicated ; but this is not believed. Trade continues uninterrupted at the Northern ports. From the Canton river we have accounts to the 22nd. The only matter reported thence is, that the Chuenpee Fort was taken possession of and occupied on the 18th instant by a portion of her Majesty's naval force. The place had been deserted, and the guns were all buried. At Hong-Kong all remains quiet. In business transactions continue as they have been for some time.

An award of 81,000 has been obtained against Allum (who was tried a short time since for having attempted to poison the community) for damages sustained by a party from having eaten of the poisoned bread from his shop on the 16th of January last. The decision on the law point, however, is, we believe, reserved.

The following telegraphic message was received from Valentin on Wednesday (Aug. 12) : þÿ "An accident of some description has occurred to the Atlantic cable. Up to 4 o'clock in the morning of yesterday (Tu esday) constant signals and messages had been received, in one of which, received some 20 hours previously, it was stated that the ship had arrived in the two miles depth. At 4 a.m. (Irish time) the electric signals suddenly ceased. On testing for insulation there was found to he a total loss, which from indications of resistance would seem to have occurred at a distance of from 350 to 400 miles from Valentin. In the absence of any means of communication with the ships it is, of course, impossible even to guess at the cause of embarrassment ; there is, however, quite sufficient room for hope at present that the loss of insulation may have been caused by some injury to a portion being payed into the water hut not dissevered from the re mainirig portion of the cable, and that they will he enabled, hy the aid ofappliances on board, to haul in and repair so much of it as will re-establish con# tinuity and instillation. RETURN OF THE SHIPS. Plymouth, Frid y Evening. The United States' steam-frigate Niagara, Captain Hudson, from the Atlantic, followed hy the Susquehanna, Captain Sands, and her Majesty's screw steamship Agamemnon, Master Commander Noddall, entered the Sound this afternoon on their return from their unsuccessful effort to lay the telegraph cable. Oil board the Niagara they report that at the time of the severance, a quarter to 4 o'clock on Tuesday morning. 335 nautical or about 380 statute miles had been laid, at a distance of 260 to 280 miles io a direct course from Valentia. The wind was Southerly, there was some sea, and the ship was going from three to fo r knots, and the cable paying out five to six, and sometimes seven, knots. As the quantity of slack thus expended was greater than expected at starting, and more than could he afford-

ed, the retard strain was therefore increased to a presure of 3,000 pounds, and the calde broke. The extra expenditure of slack commenced on Monday evening, when n strong breeze and heavy swell prevailed, and a powerful undercurrent was experienced. This current forced the wire from the ship at a considerable angle. When the break was applied with increased power the stern of the Niagara was down in the trough of a sea, and the extra strain created hy her rising was the immediate cause of the cable's parting. The Susquehanna was a mile offon the Niagara's starboard beam ; the Agamemnon, the Cyclops and the Leopard, were within signal distance. At 12 o'clock the Cyclops left for Valentin and the Leopard for Spittle. id. The oilier three remained to make some experiments. Soundings were found hy the Cyclops at 2,000 fathoms. At night they kept a course E.S.E., under easy steam, and on Wednesday morning at 10 o'clock (tore up for Plymouth Sound. The Niagara is gone into Union ize. The general opinion is that the season is too far advanced for another effort now, but every confidence is expressed in the ultimate success of the undertaking. The machinery now aboard the Niagara is considered too heavy for the purpose. It is stated that the wheels ceased to revolve when the pressure was applied on Tuesday morning. « « þÿ F K V E R -P O I S 0 N 3.

There is one point of view in which the Indian mutiny has not yet been considered by our people Admitting that the English have pursued an unprincipl. d course ot hlibusterism in the acquisition of territory, and a very oppressive and tyrannical policy in their method of retaining it, it cannot nevertheless be denied that they have conferred some benefits on India by their rule. Of late years especially, honest and well meant efforts have been made to introduce European civilization into the country; works of irrigation have been undertaken on a large scale ; railroads and telegraphs have been established ; roads for the conveyance of produce from the interior to the seaboard have been projected and even commenced ; an administration of justice þÿ doubt, but yet far superior to the native courts þÿ has been solidly planted; large and beneficial improvements have been made in the Hindoo laws concerning land tenures, marriages and wills. Under ordinary circumstances, the effect of these and the other similar improvements which are going on would, in fifty years, make of India a far greater country than she has ever been. If, however, the present insurrection is to succeed, and the English are to be driven out, these works of civilization cease, all internal improvements are stopped, and India relapses first into anarchy, next into a desolate barbarism. Again, the possession of India, and the in-

Conway several seamen lately belonging to the Schooner Endeavour, of this port, arrived here from (Jarthagena, via St. Thomas. They report a frightful

South American Coast upon the master and crew of that vessel. The 41 Emleavour" left Kingston on Tuesday the 16th June, having cleared out for Maracaibo. A few days after she experienced very severe weather, carrying away her jio3tay and topsails. She was forced to put into the port of Ansv d'Harnault, on the south west coast of Hayti. She remained there and repaired, and sailed two days after for her destination. The weather was again boisterous, and the Schooner having again carried away some sails sh p it into Cape La Vela on the Main, vv.,era :r injuries were repaired. Captain \ v Duraut had three Indians on h aa I ' ii h : had brought to Jamaica .. .. A return from the Main, i > i was shewn them by the cupiauj, .v,,o in fact was always kind towards them, even while in Kingston. The vessel arrived off the Indian Coast on patriots exiled by despotisms. Were England the evening of the 8th July ; and came to Bay Honda, to which place the Indians on board belonged. The Indians were immediately landed, and about seven o'clock the next morning a boat loaded with Indians, to the number of 15 boarded the Schooner ; and lined the gang-way. The captain, not imagining any danger from their presence, was wholly unprepared for an attack and was speakiug near by to one of the seamen, when suddenly some seven of the Indians simultaneously drew their knives (which were hid in their

girdles) and commenced to assassinate the captain; they inflicted numerous slabs all over his body, which soon brought him to the ground in a senseless state, the blood coursing along his body in a profuse manner. He made several ineffectual attempts at resistance. The cook, who was in the galley preparing breakfast, was also ah tacked by them and killed, with scarcely any chance of resistance ; meanwhile, the mate, Mr. Maduro, was personally engaged with two of the Indians, who dealt him a severe blow over the head ; but with an almost unexampled degree of strength, he held each by the throat with his hands, and bringing himself 011 his knees, he throttled them in such a manner as when he let go his hold they staggered. The panic on board among the seamen was intense ; and no one being prepared for such an encounter, the confusion and horror which prevailed at the time may better be imagined than described. A white sailor, seeing the helpless state of the crew, immediately jumped overboard, followed by a young boy, who was on board ; and they took to the boat which was alongside ; another young man named Lewis Lacoste, of this city, who had been taking a sea voyage for the benefit of his health, was the third person who left the vessel. He jumped overboard, and not being able to swim, sank, and rose no more ! Another seaman from the vessel succeeded in getting into the boat. The mate, after the wrestling with the two Indians, and seeing no other chance for his life, made one desperate leap

from the ship and was soon in the boat He cut the painter, which held the Indians' boat alongside the vessel ; and the four parties set to work with the paddles. The " Endeavour's" boat was ashore with three of her hands in her ; and these, perceiving what was going on, shoved off, and met the Indiau boat, (a whaling boat belonging to the brig Radiant , strauded some time ago off the same coast, which contained the four who had left the ship) and joined her þÿ sending the Endeavour' » boat adrift. Meanwhile the steward, who was in the hold of the vessel when this sanguinary proceeding commenced, was and these blood-thirsty assassins set upon bv soon fell a corpse, from the thrusts of the Indian knives. The Indians sacked the vessel and plundered all the stores and provisions ; and as was subsequently ascertained ran the vessel ashore. The boat with the seven souls which survived this sad tragedy, after pulling against the wind some sixty miles, fell in with some vessels, and got refreshed ; and some canvass having been provided them, they set sail the next morning and reached Rio de la Harcha in safety ; where they communicated with the Consul. They remained there for fully three weeks; and took passage for Santa Martha ; thence to Oarthagena; and from that place, they went on to St. Thomas, and arrived at Kingston on Saturday in the R. M. S. Conway. Captain Durant was a trader to the Spanish Main for upwards of 30 yearR ; and had endeared himself to many of the natives. He failed on this melancholy oc-

casion to observe the necessary precaution of not allowing more than a certain number to come on board at one time ; and this fatal error on his part has led to the sacrifice both of valuable lives and of property to some amount. The captain, however, was too coi.fident of the good feeling of the natives towards him ; so much so that he forgot to arm himself to repel their attack. The steward was a native of this city, and the cook a Frenchman. The Endeavour was owned by S. M Samuels, Esq., of this city.

ASSASSINATION OF MR. SULIVAN, THE BRITISH MINISTER. PERU. Dates from Callao are to August 12. The painful news of the assassination of S. E. Sulivan, Esq., British Minister at Lima, will be found in our correspondent's letter, and the account, as given in the Comcrdo of Lima, we publish in our Spanish part, not having room for a translation to-day. The conduct of the Peruvian officials towards American vessels, lias called for the interference of the United States Minister, who, no doubt, witli his usual promptitude, will demand redress. Private letters assure us that the presence of an American vessel-of-war is very much needed at the present time on the coast. News has just been sent from Lima that

Mr. Sulivan, the British Minister, was assassinated by six Peruvians. The Vixen has gone to Paita in search of Admiral Bruce. It is supposed that he was murdered for the British interference in the matter ol the Tom bin and Lou. I have just received the particulars of the affair: Mr. Sulivan was dining alone, when six men, masked, entered and fired three shots, one of which is fatal, having entered the groin and passed up in the lungs. Alter the deed them exclaimed þÿ " I am now satisfied," was done one of and then they all disappeared. As yet no one is suspected for it. Callao, Aug. 12, 3 p.m. A Frenchman and a negro have been just arrested on suspicion of being accomplices of the assassination of Mr. Sulivan.

It is scarcely possible to contemplate the sublime spectacle now presented iu all. its startling grandeur to the reflection of the world without wonder and awe. That 50,000 Europeans, standing in the midst of 120,000,000 of Asiatics whom they have wronged and conquered, should crush their rebellion arid throttle treason out of them þÿ that, isolated and surrounded in a strange land and uncongenial climate, with countless enemies on every side, they should, with hut a stamp of their imperious foot, tread out the flames of revolt, and regard their supremacy as a settled destiny that, tats' itself cannot alter ; that is, indeed, a climax of the majesty of character and mind without parallel in the annals of the human race. THE INDIAN MUTINY. It is quite necessary, in such a crisis as that which our Eastern empire is passing through, that we should express our coDvietiotis of causes, our views ol events and our ideas of future policy, in p'ain and unmistakeahle words Open as the columns of this Journal arc to many shades ot liberal opinion, and anxious as are those who conduct it that no voice shall be stifled or repressed which tells its own truth on behalf of the gieat interests of humanity, we are bound editorially to be practical should and to enforce what rather than speculative, be done by the authority of what wc see and know

First, for British dominion in India. It is quite true that much of it has been acquired by conquest, and that the occasions of warfare are to be justified by the morality which prevailed iu the politics of the last age, rather than by the higher principle which we would exert every nerve and saorifice every advantage to see fairly dominant in this. But accepting the heritage of our fathers, we may honestly declare that it is, aocording to the law of their time, an honourable one, which we need not be ashamed to maintain And as all cessions must have a result in the substitution of the party in whose favour they are made, we can distinctly declare that no party, European or Asiatic, would succeed us in our rule of India without inflicting a change immeasurably for the worse upon the present, and still tnore upon the future of the population. Of European nations we are by far the most liberal, humane and unselfish in our dealings with subject races ; as to Asiatic Prinoes, their dominion would be tyranny, chequered with revolt, massacre and anarchy. Henceforth, more than ever, public opinion in England must guide the administration of Hindostan, and the people here will be the effeotive, and we trust the sincere and intelligent guardians of the people there With regard to the supposed injuries of native Princes, there scarcely exist any chiefs whose rights are of a creation antecedent to our own. They are usually the descendants of successful usurpers of recent date who have rent authority

from more apparently legitimate masters, themselves the effete, besotted, luxurious, degraded heirs of former adventurers who have won their authority by no other means than that of supplanting worn-out dynasties The Mahomedans ware the fierce conquerors of the Hindoo race, and were bitter oppressors in all religious, if not ail oivil matters. Their reign does not date bo far back as to make thoir usurpation venerable, or to oloak it with the oustom of ages- The few things we are bound to respcot are the ancient local self-government of the native villages, a model of primitive law, police and social custom, and the religious oonvictions of all parties. This ground we are bound to take up in the face of that envy and hatred which make mouths at us from every despotic State and faction in Europe. England has errors and sins of administration to regret and atone for ; but the England of this day needs to feel little remorse for its intentions, and is rather to be reproached for a lacy backwardness in carrying them out than a refusal to recognize the obligations of justice. We stand indomitably firm, then, to thereconquest of India, if reconquest it must be, at the expence of every ship, every shilling, every man. that may be needed for the work. This great and noble country, the only stronghold in Europe for all that is endowed with the hope of progress, the only powerful State that avows and maintains political principles worthy of the aims of human nature, cannot be beaten, and

will not in a struggle for its own position of mastery and independent strength. Every Englishman will take his stand to live or die on that ground. As an Asiatic Power we are bound by the same law. Speaking for the people of Iudia, we have no successor capable of taking our place, of performing the duty we owe, which wo nave been more and more willing, if not anxious to pay for years past, and which we now, more than ever see the necessity of carrying out to the letter. We will not resign or delegate our funotions- We intend to rule in India, and for the welfare of the Indians. If any enemies, open or concealed, endeavour to thwart us in that, resolve, we must combat them to the death and not be satisfied without leaving a mark upon them they can never forget or efface. We are strong enough to do it ; if we were not, we should not constitute this British commonwealth. As to the mode of putting down the rebellion, it is worse than needless for us here to argue as if we were to inoitc or direct the retribution. The deeds which will be done in India are far beyond the control of any moral power in England. There will bo blood enough, vengeance enough, savagery enough, crime enough in punishing crime. We are not to be repelled by any reproach of " maudlin humanity" set forth in such a journal as the Times þÿ the pander to any feeling, good or bad, that reigns fiercely around it, the worshipper of any opinion endowed with £ s d. þÿ from urging such moderation in the awful retribution to eome as it befits men in
every circumstance to show. We see no symp-

t r. e i » i x « » tom of courage in urging massacre from the safe purlieus of Fleetstreet. We look upon incentives to blood as the signs of cowardice, of fear, of spite excited by terror We regret deeply to see letters from Iudia, written, too, by officers, dwelling on the necessity, not of stern justice, but of indiscriminate slaughter. They are, perhaps, the very pardonable ebullitions of indignation, uot the cool resolves of firmheartedness. Does anybody doubt that there will be extermination enough ? Docs any one think that be needs prompt the soldier in the assault to waste of life and cruelty in taking it ? Blame him we certainly shall not, any more than the Times. Those who are in India have seen the horrors we shudder at in having them hinted to us in writing or in print, or in whispered speech. We shall neither wonder at nor reproach any merciless retribution. The deeds that compel military execution being beyond mere narrative, are utterly beyond the heightening of rhetoric. They must be paid for in degree, and caDnot be atoned sufficiently. But we shall not be ashamed if any word of ours can avert a needless wound, or save a fellow-being, though an Indian, from a fiendish torment. We utterly and with all our soul despise and abhor instigations to cruelty. If we are included in what is meant for censure or sneer by the instigators we are honoured. Onoe again, is it possible for us to contend with the revolters in the villainy of infliction ? If not, let us cede that superiority and assert our

own in another fashion. Next we come to the polioy to be pursued after the subjugation of revolt. There are those who are looking to the annihilation of native customs, and the active discouragement if not persecution of native creeds. We have surely to retreat rather than to go forward in this regard. We have, in a country jealous of religion, earnest in it to a degree which few Europeans of any race, creed, or class can equal, prostituted the apparent influence and patronage of the ruling Power to a futile attempt at conversion. No doubt can now remain that this is a religious revolt. "Religion" is the cry and the cause of the mutineers, the watchword that forbids them to spare life, that goads them to miscreant devilry, as it has so often done in Europe That we have provoked and brought about the belief that we intented to force or cheat the ratives into Christianity, is a fact that bears its own condemnation. We have, at the least, made a most grievous blunder. We have it now upon the fullest authority that our Queen herself was supposed to have rejoiced in the device of the cartridges, as a means to bring about that apostacy in the Hindoos which their Mahomedan conquerors had in so many instanoes heretofore compelled. We have bad too many parson Generals, and too many women in petticoats as well as in breeohes, affecting to discountenance the old religion and introduce a superior one. The missionaries would have been tolerated, as long is they had only taught and

reisoned. The ludian does not flinch from argument, but he does not expect to be browbeaten by a ridiculous affectation of exclusive sanctity. He allows another to believe what he will, and tell his belief; and he claims the same right. If, then, any missionary action is hence forth permitted in India, it must be confined strictly within the bouuds of lecturing. It must have no Government countenance, beyond the civil protection accorded to all. Sectarian schools must not be heard of. Nor will true Christianity lose a jot by the restraint. The Hindoo observes. He is much sooner taught by example than by preoept. If he could see Christians acting up to their profession, he would honour, and possibly, might believe them. Let his own creed be debased as it may, he fully acts upon it. Little indeed, therefore, has boen done in changing it for the pseudo-belief of those who, strictly speaking, act as though they had none. The old complaoency of the irreligious adventnrer, the officer of half a century ago, who respected native ceremonies and actively countenanced them, was every way better and wiser administration than our modern metbodism. If there be a true Christian spirit ever inspired into India, it will prevail by the very reverse of bigotry, narrowmindedness, fanaticism, supercilious assumption of infallibility, contempt for native belief It will make the best of what it finds, not despise it. The very usages which are decidedly immoral and antisocial should have been removed by a hand of very different skill
from that which has dealt with tbem

With regard to our annexations, they must be firmly maintained, and their value to the ruled proved by a good Government that does not disdain to explain its acts and appeal to the understanding of its subjects How is it possible to avoid discontent rising occasionally to revolt, when the very language of the governed it not used or understood by the governors ? In a most interesting and clearly written letter from Chuuar, we have an account of the resistance of the 37th Native Infantry aud the Sikhs at Benares, arising altogether from the incapacity of the officers to explain to the soldiery, that, on delivering up their arms, they were not subjecting themselves to be put to death. They saw European troops before them ready to fire, and by the mere instinct of manly resistance- to slaughter, they retained their own muskets, and used them. They fired because they believed they were to be subject to wanton execution Is it possible that systematic unfitness and inea pacity can go further than in bringing about explain an apparently murderous threat bloody rebellion for the want of the power to ' All Continental Europe, as well as every thinker among ourselves, has doomed the double Government. The Queen's power must administer the Queen's justice, and one rapidly obeyed authority must control all iu India. The Circumlocution Office is no substitute for autocratio resolve It will not be enough to alter a name ; we have to substitute a good system for one never allowed to grow to good. But this

will be a fruitful theme for other discussions One example we point to in another artiole will show that we are not advocating the Royal administration as it is. Ncgligeuco, selfishness and faction have left all to amend. It is well if we have the courage to enter upon the task and the energy worthily to complete it.

Death of Eugene Sue. þÿ This celebrated writer died on Monday morning, at. Annecy, in Savoy, where he had resided for some time. Eugene Sue was the son of a celebrated French surgeon of that name, whose greatest claim to celebrity lies in a curious controversy in which he was once engaged relative to the painfulness or painlessness of the punishment of death by the guillotine. The future novelist himself served for some time in a medical capacity in the Royal Marine of France, and we have a memento of his maritime experiences in the shape of a ponderous History of the French Navy, now little remembered and less read. When about 30 years of age, M. Sue came to settle in Paris, and devoted himself to literary pursuits. His earlier works, "Pauline." "The Watch tower of Koat-Ven," and the " Female Blue Beatd," acquired lor him a consider able reputation as a melodramatic writer ; his extraordinary romance, the " Myste but it was not till the publication of ries of Paris," in 1842-3, that he attained that eminence as a writer of fiction, which made even the great masters of that branch of art, Soulie and Dumas, tremble at the popularity of their dangerous rival. The "Mysteries" were followed sensation, " The Wandering Jew," which by a novel which created even a greater was remarkable not only for its enthralling interest as a romance, but for the peculiar political views therein for the first time developed by the author. These works brought enormous sums to Eugene Sue.

For "The Wandering Jew" alone he is stated to have received no less a sum than ceeded " Martin ; or the Memoirs of a Valet 150,000 francs, or £6,000. To these sucde Chambre," and " The Seven Capital Sins," and some works of minor interest. From the period of the revolution of 1848, Eugene Sue threw himself entirely into politics. He was a member of the revolutionary assemblies of that stormy era ; and though, after his proscription, he still showed himself occasionally in print, from his retreat at Annecy in Savoy, his works were more political pamphlets than novels.

(From the Bermuda linyal Gazette, Sept 1 ) FATAL EXPLOSION OF A POWDER M AGAZI N E. Halifax, Friday, August 14. The merchants powder magazine containing the whole stock of powder in Halifax, exploded with a terrific concussion shortly after midnight, last night. One man was killed and fifteen others were seriously injured. Five houses were demolished and several d amaged. The Government magazine and the new Barracks w, re much shattered, and nearly all the windows in the northern part of the city were broken. The damages are estimated at $100,000 The magazine is supposed to have been fired by an incendiary. For hours the excitement was intense, many persons had been thrown from their beds, and others bewildcrod, rushed to the streets for safety, believing an earthquake had occurred.

Harris, surgeon to the Khtrsontse steam-ship, writes to the Lancet : þÿ "I am much surprised at the opinion which is so prevalent of the utter incurability of sea-sickness. I believe this opinion to exist amongst the non-medical part of the community from sheer ignorance, and amongst sea-going surgeons from a supineness in applying remedies, a fault to which they are rather too subject. As surgeon to one of the firstclass American steam-ships, which each voyage carries over to Portland at least 400 emigrants, I think I may venture to state my experience. In the greater number of instances I allow the stomach to discharge its contents one or twice, I and then, if there is no organic disease, give five drops of chloroform in a little water, and, if

(From the Jamaica Despatch.) THE CUBAN SLAVE TRADE. It has been suggested by a Londou pa per that the safest and most certain mode of abolishing the Cuban Slave Trade would be to indoctrinate the commercial spirit into the present inland traders in human flesh, and to convince them by the very palpable influence to pecuniary gain that it is better to trade in Ivory, Palmoil and Pindar nuts, than to depart and sell the human machinery by which alone this merchandise is obtainable in adequate quantity. The Press þÿ which is the one member of the fraternity that has alone set its face against any positive effort on the part of England to suppress the ocean traffic by means of a well-organised blockade of the Cuban Coast, þÿ is manifestly ignorant of the machinery by which Africa, in its present state, can alone become extensively commercial. It is generally assumed that, but for the Slave Trade, Africa would present a Continent of free, and happy, but uncivilized and little industrious human beings. It is imagined that the slavery that proceeds from Africa is simply and wholy the result of warfare between tribes ; aud that this warfare is stimulated, if not produced, by the demand for slaves on the Coast for ex- Eortation. ut for the mart which the Cuban, or any In effect, it is imagined that, other ocean Slave Trade affords there could be no slavery in Africa. There never was a greater delusion ! It is a well-known fact that slavery is the condition of the masses in Africa. With the exception of a few tribes near the

Western Coast, the general condition of the p ople is that of slavery, and slavery, too, of a most frightful character. The cti. f of a tribe not only exercises a rigid rul over the persons and services of his ti i ner >U3 slaves, but he holds their lives at his disposal and will, and it is nothing uncoin; non for fifty or a hundred, or three times the latter number, to be put to death, in order to propitiate a heathen deity or modify an evil augury. It is imagined that the Slave Trade nurses internecine warfare for the purpose of making slaves This, too, is a mistake. It is true that one of the principal trophies of African warfare among tribes consists in the number of slaves captured; but the slaves were slaves already, and it is one of the most awful characteristics of the barbarism of the African people, that, in most instances, the celebration of a victory consi ts not more in the number of slaves taken, than in the extent of human sacrifice which is made of these slaves by the victorious chiefs. The slaves that are taken down to the Coast for sate ore, generally speaking, the property of chiefs in the interior, who use them to carry down the ivory, palm oil, and other articles of export, which the Press looks to as the means of putting down the trade, and who then sell them to the owners of the slave barracoons, where carry them off This, however, they are detained until the slavers is arrive to by no means the only mode in which the slave dealers on the Coast are supplied. It is
quite notorious that among the tribes on

the Western Coast it is the commonest thing in the world for parents The chihireu to the slave dealer. to sell their cargoes of slave children, few ot them exceeding twelve or fourteen years of age, which pour into Cuba, are principally obtained in this way. Any oliicer oi the navy who has been long stationed on the Coast of Africa will confirm this statement ; and if further evidence were wanted, we have it here in this island, in the persons of young Africans who have a perfect recollection ot their being sold by their own mothers. It is a mistake, therefore, to suppose that the Slave Trade, bad as it may be, is the occasion of any increase ol internal warfare in Africa for the purpose of making slaves. The people from the interior who are sold on the Coast are slaves already þÿ they were born slaves, and they would have died slaves. All accounts agree that the native slavery of Africa is even more frightful in its personal aspect than in any civilised country, because amongst a savage people, the value of human life is little more considered than that of the humblest living thing in nature. It is because we have a perfect conviction that this is in fact the actual state of the masses of the population ol Africa, that we have urged, and continue to maintain, in spite of opposition, that one of the most essentially humane measures that could be undertaken by England, in failure of any determined effort to put down the ocean j sidering Slave Trade by force, would be to ransom

the African slave on his own 6oil btfore lie : will reached the slave ship. If it be true that 1 the slave of the barraooon is nothing more than a slave of the interior, removed to the coast, for exchange from one frightful phase of human tyranny to of another, the intermediate prospect he horrors of with the middle passage ere he can reach his ultimate destination of misery we ask any þÿ philanthropist how much we cou:d add to the wrongs of this unhappy creature were we permitted to rescue him by a money ransom from the hands of his inhuman owner, and to place him a free Britisu subject on the shores of Jamaica? We have revolved this question in our minds repeatedly, in the hope ol discovering the horrible immorality which is supp d to nestle in it, but we have never been able to detect it. If the Slave Trade were abolished to-morrow, slavery would exist still iu Africa. Instances are þÿknown and they have been cited in the of House of Com- mons on the authority naval officers þÿ of large trains ol slaves taken down to the Coast with Ivory and other merchandize from the interior of Africa having been ruthlessly put to death their owner because there was no immediate sale for them, and lie could not or would not afford either to feed them for any length of time on the Coast, or to take them back with him into the interior. Many of these trains travel upwards of a J preponderance. thousand miles to the Coast, and the owner calculates on a double traffic : he soils the ivory and palm oil to lie the calculates rican merchant, and English or Ame- j through on mak-

ing good his venture by the disposal ol his slaves to the Spaniard or Portuguese. Would it be a mercy, or a cruelty, to these poor people to buy tliern up for transport to Jamaica as free people? » þÿ Frnm the Weekly Dispatch, August 9.

RUSSIAN INTRIGUES WITH CHINA. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 15th SEPTEMBER, 1857. An election of a few new members to the Colonial Council will take place on the 26th lust. It behooves the electors to pause and consider what they have done, and what they intend to do. Complaints are heard on every side ot the inutility of the Colonial Council. Tln.se, we know, are uttered by the enemies of representative try. government " What," say they, " has the Colonial who are found in every coun- Council done tor us? We have only been taxed and taxed until we cannot be taxed any more." We readily grant, that little has been done, in a direct way, to benefit the Colonies; but we remember, at the same time, how limited the Colonial Council is in power; being but a mere shadow of representative Government. It lias but a consultative voice ; and in all the laws which have passed it, Government took the initiative. Some few bills were brought in by members, but they were all speedily smothered. Is it necessary to point out the cause of this? Let us calmly consider the question for a moment and we shall find that we have ourselves to blame in the matter. No great argument is requisite to prove that when we return members who are pledged to support the present state of things, whose very existence, we may say, depends oil the perpetuity of that state, under which alone their class-advantages are secured to them, we can never expect to see any material reform carried out. It is sheer nonsense to expect it ; for it would be suicidal in them to perform it. Look at the many

bills proposed by Government and see how readily they have been adopted. But where, are the laws which could beneiit the Colonics, and which even received the sanction of this too-willing consultative Body? We allude to the Law on the Press, the law regarding Coins and some others. Have they not been held back from passing into operation ? And has one undcrsigued begs leave to inform ttumb r of the Colonial Council ever raised A those who might otherwise be willing his voice against tue injustice of proposing laws to the people's representatives, (who warmly advised their adoption), and afterwards withholding them ? Let us be just to ourselves before we complain. Let us return such members as we think will raise their voices in favor of the Colonies ; and let us rather abstain from voting than vote for a man from selfish motives. Remember electors ! You are responsible to the Supreme Power lor every idle word that you utter. You are therefore equally responsible for your votes.

FRANCE. The trial of the men accused of the conspiracy to assassinate the Emperor of the French took place on the 6th of August, in the Cour d' Assises de la Seine. The accused were Paolo Tibaldi, Giuseppi Bartolotti, and Paolo Grilli (alias Faro), already in the hands of justice The accused Giuseppi Mazzini, Alexandre Auguste Ledru Kollin, Gactuno Massarcnti, and Frederico Campanella. The indictment is þÿ "For having, in 1857, by a resolution to act, concerted and agreed upon by themselves, iormed a plot having lor its object an attempt upon the life of the Emperor, the said plot having been followed

by an act committed, or commenced to prepare the execution of it, which crime tails within the article 89 of the penal code." The proceedings commenced threading the act of accusation. Tibaldi upon being examined denied all connection with Mazzini and his agents ; and stated that he knew nothing of the letters which had been identified. Grilli stated that Tibaldi had given him two poniards for the purpose of killing the emperor, but that he never intended to use them ; he had also received lOOOf. in Loudon. Baitolotti, the third prisoner, deposed that lie hud been taken to Mazzini's by Massarenti, from whom he got 50 Napoleons to go to Paris and kill the emperor. After the examination of some witnesses, several letters connected with the accused and the revolutionary party were read by the judge. The court then adjourned until the following morning, when the proceedings wen resumed. At length the jury retired to consider their verdict, and after deliberating for 40 minutes, found nu affirmative verdict on all the questions, but with extenuating circumstances in favour of Grilli and Bai t olotti. The court, in consequence, condemned Tibaldi to transportation, and Grilli and Bartolotti each to 15 years' imprisonment. Ledru Rollin and the other refugees in England have stoutly denied the slightest complicity in the alleged plot, and no one on this side the channel believes them to be guilty.

ITALY. The following are the principal passages of a document found at Genoa among the papers of the late Colonel Pisacane, the chief of the insurrection in Calabria. It is endorsed þÿ "This is my political will," uud is dated Genoa, June 2A, 1857 : þÿ " At the moment that I am about to risk my life in a rash undertaking, I wish to make known my opinions to the country iu order to combat the criticisms of the vulgar, ever disposed to applaud the victors landing, which will be Sapri, I will conand to execrate the vanquished. My political opinions are sufficiently known þÿ I believe in Socialism, but in a different Socialism from the French systems, all more or less founded on the monarchical and despotic idea which prevails in the nation. on the country and not on me. I have The Socialism to which I allude may be comprised in the two words ' liberty' and and I hesitate not to do it. I am convinced 'association.' I have developed this opinion in two volumes which I composed þÿ the fruit of nearly six years' study, and to which, for want of time, I have not been approve beforehand any but vulgar plans. able to give the last touch as regards style and diction. If some one of my friends would replase me and publish these two volumes, I would be extremely grateful to crossing the Atlantic with such bouts. him. 1 am convinced that railways, electric telegraphs, machinery, improvements in manufactures þÿ in fact, all that developes and facilitates commerce, is destined by an inevitable law to impoverish the mass of

the people until a division of the profits is made by competition. All these means increase production, but they accumulate them in a small number of hands, from which it results that this so much vaunted

9 T.. ft ft ft ti ft ft V I 9 progress is, in fact, only decadence. If these pretended meliorations are regarded as a progress, it will be in this þÿsense tl at by increasing the misery of the people they will infallibly impel them to a terrible revolution, which, by changing social order, will turn to the advantage of all that which now serves for the profit of a few 1 am convinced that Italy will become great by liberty, or will be a slave. I am convinced that temperate remedies such as the constitutional system in Piedmont and the progressive improvements granted to Lombardy, far from advancing the regeneration of Italy, can only retard it. As for myself, I would not make the smallest sacrifice to change a Ministry or to obtain a constitution þÿ not even to drive the Austrians out of Lombardy and to unite that province to the kingdom of Sardinia. In my opinion the domination of the house of Savoy and the domination of tiie House of Austria are precisely the same thing. I believe, likewise, that the constitutional system in Piedmont is more injurious to Italy than the tyranny of Ferdinand II. I believe firmly that if Piedmont had been governed in the same manner as the other States of Italy the revolution of Italy would have been effected at the present day. This, my decided opinion, arises from the profound conviction I entertain that the propagation of an idea is a chimera ; that the instruction of a people is an absurdity. Ideas are derived from facts, and not taciS from ideas, and a nation will not be t ee

because it is educated, but it will very soon become educated when it si. all be free. The only act a citizen can pi il.uni in order to be uselul to his country is to wait patiently for an opportunity to cooperate in a material revolution. Conspiracies, plots, attempts at insurrection are, in my opinion, the series of facts through which Italy is moving towards her object þÿ unity. With my principles I would have thought I hud omitted a sacred duty if, seeing the possibility of attempting a surprise on a wellchoseu point and under favourable circumstances, I had not employed all my energy in executing it, and in bringing it to a successful conclusion. I do not pretend to be the saviour of my country, though ui.uiy idlers, for their own justification, hud uccused me of so pretending. No; but I a n convinced that a moral insurrection exists in the South of Italy, that an energetic impulse might drive the population to attempt a decisive movement, and it is for that reason my efforts are employed to accomplish a conspiracy which will give this impulse If I arrive at the place of

sider I have gaiued a great personal success, should I afterwards die on the scaffold. A simple individual though I am, supported by a great number of generous men, I can do more, and if I do so the rest will depend
only my life to sacrifice for such an object, that if the enterprise succeed I shall obtain universal applause. If I fail the public will blame me. The world never
The man was called mad who first tried a steamboat in America, and the impossibility was subsequently demonstrated by

Our Columbus was a madman before ho discovered America, and the vulgar would have called Hannibal and Napoleon madmen had they succumbed, the one at Trebia, and the other at Marengo. I do not pretend to compare my undertaking with that of those great men. It resembles theirs, however, in one point of view, for it will be the object of universal disapprobation if I fail, and of the admiration of the

world it I succeed. If Napoleon, before h,' quirted Elba to land at Frejus with 50 Grena. iters, had asked advice, his plan would have been unanimously blamed Napoleon had what I have not, the prestige of his name; but I rally round my flag all the affections and all the hopes of the Italian revolutionists. All the griefs and all the miseri 's of Italy will fight on my side. I have b.i, « ne word more to say. If I do not succeed 1 profoundly despise tin; ignoble vulgar who will condemn me. II 1 succeed I will very little appreciate their applause. I will find my reward in my conscience and in the approbation of those dear and generous friends who afforded me their assistance, and who participated in the beating of my heart and in my hopes. Nhould our sacrifice produce no advantage to Italy, it will nevertheless be a glory for her to have produced children who desired to sacrifice themselves for her future prosperity. " Charles Pisacane."

PRUSSIA. The Prussian Government, in reply to questions put on the subject, has officially declared its full approval of the conduct of the Prussian Commissioner in the Danubian Principalities. The Governments of the Zollverein demand collectively from England, through the medium of Prussia, an indemnification for the losses incurred by their fellow-subjects at Canton, the bombardment having taken place without a notification having been made to rhe Consuls.

NESB1T (Continued ) Another experiment is that of a celebrated French chemist, who placed a living branch of a vine in a glass tube, and then covered the tube all over with blackened paper, so that no light could penetrate, and he sent a current of air through it containing about five per cent, of carbonic-acid gas. He sent th s through the tube, and did not expose it to the light. He found that the tube at the other end, which passed through the lime-water, gave an abundant precipitate, showing that ihe leaves had no action n the charcoal gas. He then took off the paper, and exposed the tube and vinebranch to the light of the sun; and on now sending the stream of air and carbonic acid through the apparatus, not a trace of carbonic acid was found to pass through at the other end. A. .other point which you have to remember is, that plants obtain the largest amount of tbeir nutriment from the air. You shall plant a forest upon land which contnins no vegetable matter þÿ I might say, upon Brown Willy or Rough Tod ; you, or some one else coming after you, may, at the end of say fifty years, remove cart-load after cart-load of timber, and yet, at the expiration of the period, the soil shall be richer in vegetable matter than it was when the trees were first planted. \ here did all this vegetable matter come from, if not from the air ? Again, in the case of a field of turnips, it is the action of the leaves of toe turnip upon the air that secures the greatest amount of vegetable matter. Bear in mind,

then, that plants are dependent in a far greater degree upon the air than upon the land j that so far as the land is concerned, you can only, after a due upply of mineral matter, assist the plant in endeavouring io obtain more organic matter by its roots from the land than it could naturally obtain by its leaves from the air; and in 'his consists the true principle of manuring. I inu t i.o ceed to speak to you about the production ot farmyard dung. 'J hat is the sine ?ua ariners attach too much importance to it, non of farmers, and 1 am afraid that some regard it as if nothing else could equal it in value. Now, gentlemen, what is farm-yard dung? I am not about to speak now of all the various modes of manuring which are adopted.

though I have heard it stated that the decomposing vegetatde matter differs greatly in different countries. Farmyard dung is neither more nor less than decomposed vegetable matter, derived from plants which once had life in the soil, and which, when returned to the land, will furnish the necessary elements for reproducing vegetable life. The manner in which it is decomposed þÿ the mode of reducing it to n proper state for its application to the þÿland is quite another question. Is what 1 have heard stated true, that in Devon shire and Cornwall there are partie- who are in the habit of strewing t eir straw on the highroads and bye-roads 1 Is it true that in this country it is the practice to place vegetable tnitter in a position in which everythii g in it that is valuable is likely to i e washed awrr i If that is 'lie mode of making laitn-v id manure which is adopted in this district, or in o'her d is ricts, all I can say with regard to it is, that it is not a mode which 1 should recommend for imitation Gentlemen, in considering the snl ject of the decomposition of vegetable matters, you must remember that some elements of vegetables aie volatile, and some soluble, and that th se w icli are least volatile aim least soluble are also least valuahi 'I he substance in manures which is mos» volatile is ammonia; and where there is bad management this will pass away into the air; while the potash and the soda, and the other soluble materials, wdl be washed a way. As compa ed

with the practice which I have mentioned, would it not be well to put your straw in the farm-yard sheltered from wet, and place your feeding animals upon it ? because, in that ca.-e, you would have the dung of the animals upon the straw, and the vegetable matter also. 'J lie truth is, that every possible precaution ought to be taken against losing anything valuable that is contained in vegetable matter ; and with this view you should seek to have a proer amount of moisture and no more, and eneavour to associate farm-yard manure with materials which will tend to fix the ammonia, and so on, and prevent it from passing away. Now the quality of the manure must depend on the quality of the vegetables on which you feed your animals. If you feed them merely upon straw, the value of the dung will le in proportion to that of the straw ; whereas, if you add oilcake, and other su. stances of a similar nature, there will be a propn tionate intrease of value. There is no ultimate action in the animal ec nomy þÿ no action, that is, in relation to the food which the animal consumes, that does not take place in ordinaiy decomposition. If you decomposed a large quantity of veget ible matter, whether it we e oilcake or straw, vou would have just the same ultimate result r.s if you passed it through the body of an animal. J'be animal system does not add anything whatever to its value ; the animal only gives forth what it received. Indeed, so far as manuring is concerned, the dung ot the animal is always less valuable than

would have been the food on which the animal had subsisted It must, therefore, always be borne in mind by practical fanners that the animal adds nothing to food, but only subtracts from it. Many persons are apt to imagine that the fact is otherwise ; but they are certainly mistaken. If you had more turnips than your sheep þÿrequired and I have known such an instance and were to chop up a field of turnips and ploiig i them in, the result would be that you would afterwards get a far better barley crop than you would have done had sheep, by eating them, robbed the turnips of a po rtion of their value. 1 have seen that experiment tried over and over again, and it has always been attended with the same result ; therefore theory and practice perfectly coincide in this matter. Well, now, with respect to the making of farm-yard manure, let me impress upon you that, so far as the quality is ooncemed, that depends on the food of the animal ; and that in order to its conservation you must protect it against water. It is my opinion that, with the view of most effectually preserving the ammonia, you had better make a kind of compost heap, first spreading a quantity of ditch stuff, road scrapings, or other oaTtbly matter, and then putting a layer of dung, then another layer of earth, and s> on, alternating tho oartli with the dung in such a manner as will he most likely to cau-e the earth to absorb the substances which wonld otherwise t»«s into the air, and to prevent tho

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX FRIDAY, 2Sth AUGUST, 1857. Our Querist " Alpha" has thrown upon us the burden of replyitig to a question which we would rather see answered by those who ought to be, more interested in obtaining public opinion, on that subject, than we can be supposed to be. If it is an object to the elected members of the Burgher Council to hear public opinion on their acts, in that capacity, especially on so important a one as the expenditure of the public money, no better means could he employed to obtain that end, than tbe publishing of the yearly Budget, in preference to the yearly statement of expenses See., 'formerly published ; since, in the, former case, the public could remonstrate against an expense before it took place, while, in the latter case, the trouble might be saved, since it would he idle to remonstrate against what has already been done. That the publication of this Budget might interest our subscribers, wo entertain no reasonable doubt. So would a list of a merchant's newly-imported merchandize ; and any similar advertisement. But no one, in his senses, would require us to do this without payment. Our stock of public work is considerably diminished, as we cannot execute it as cheap as the Printing Offices in Copenhagen. Even tbe Burgher Council prefers to have its blank receipts lithog aplied at the Government's private lithographic office, than to pay the expense ol having them printed. '1 his forces on us the necessity to be just to those whom we employ, before we are generous to the public.

The Burgher Council is responsible to its Constituents. We are not to our Subscribers. He who cares not to keep our paper, will not wait to be told that he may discontinue it. If the members of the Burgher Council do not care to defray the expenses of the publication of the Budget, we ought to be excused from performing that duty f r them; although the false, plea is advanced that we thereby might please our subscribers No doubt of it ! But if our subscribers cannot be pleased without seeing us ruined, then we are sorry that they will not be, if we can help it. It is surprising to us, but no less the fact, that all the advantages which other countries derive from the possession of elective bodies

are totally wanting in ours. The rule seems to be that we must be taxrd, pay our taxes quietly, and tamely submit to whatever application of the public money our elected r aresentatives (1 J deem proper. Is it any wonder that no public opinion exists 1 To us the greater wonder would be the existence of such an opinion in connection with the peculiar disadvantages under which we labour
The Proceedings of the Burgher Council's meeting, held on the 10th inst., were received too late for to-day's issue, but will appear in our next.

SPAIN. The law on the Spanish press, the execution of which the Narvaez Cabinet demanded as a matter of urgency, is now in full force. The Madrid journals have the signature of the writer at the bottom of each article. The Government does not relax in the severity of its measures. On Friday Senor Llorente, ex-deputy in the Constituent Cortes, was arrested and lodged in tbe citadel of Seu d'Urgel. The reas( n of his arrest is not stated. Although order is said to be everywhere re-established, the Government is causing detachments of troops to visit different districts. At Malaga and the neighbourhood, too, the authorities are, by its direction, looking :A revolutionists who are in hiding; r. : . has ordered a judicial functionary oi '.v to proceed to Utrera and other piacts, f order to ascertain the share which the populations had in the recent revolt.

AMERICA. The steam-ship Empire City had arrived at New York with dates from Havannah to the 9th July. The Spanish war vessels in port had been ordered on a cruise. Upon the information of the English Consul, General Concha had ordered the arrest of some merchants in Puerto Principe on a charge of landing slaves. There was no news of General Santa Anna. Sugars were firm. The stock of molasses light. The stock of sugar in Havannah and Mantanzas was 5,000 hog-heads and 325,000 boxes. The New York Herald's correspondent at Sagna la Grande writes : þÿ " Two barques from the West Coast of Africa succeeded in landing off this place, on the night of the 24th instant, 950 slaves, and both vessels were under canvass the following morning before sunrise for Brazil. The British Consul forwarded a letter stating the occurrences to the Governor of Jamaica, who has ordered a British frigate to go in pursuit of the slavers."

The completion of the manufacture and stowage of the cable which shall hereafter unite the Old and New World was celebrated last week by a fete cliampetre, given at the Belvedere, near Erith, trie picturesque seat of Sir Culling Eardley. The guests invited to this festival of science were the artisans who have been engaged upon the great work, with their wives and families ; a large party of the officers, with the sailors, from the Agamemnon ; and a number of distinguished visitors. A sumptuous cold collation was provided for the 200 guests by Mr. Staples. Sir Culling Eardley presided ; and at the conclusion of the repast the usual loyal toasts and speeches expressive of the unity and cordial feeling which exist between this country and America followed, and were most enthusiastically received. Mr. Cyrus Field, one of the principal promo-

ters of the great plan, in returning thanks, read a letter which he had received front the President of the United States in which Mr. Buchanan warmly expressed his sense of the honour which it would be to him to receive the first message on the completion of the undertaking ; and this, Mr. Field said, it had been arranged should be sent from this side of the Atlantic, by no less a personage than her Most Gracious Majesty. Mr. Glasse, the maker of the Greenwich half of the cable, in a few well-chosen remarks adverted to the manufacturing difficulties which had to be overcome in the completion of such a gigantic work within so brief a period, the contract having only been made last January, and 2600 miles in all being now finished, shipped, and ready for the fulfilment of their great international duties. The dinner for the remainder of the guests, 726 in number, was supplied by Mr. Baker, of the Rosherviile Hotel, Gravesend. The completion of one half of the cable by Messrs. Newall and Co was celebrated at their works, Birkenhead, last month, by a dinner given to about 600 of their workmen, with their wives and families. The shipping of the great cable has been a gigantic labour, of which we illustrate that portion which was executed at East Greenwich. Here the Agamemnon was moored off the wharf at Glasse and Elliot's yard. She had anything but a sightly aspect, the dead weight of the cable and the rather ponderous appliances for paying it out having altered her trim appearance

for the worse. In the large Engraving of the vessel in the present Number the wire is being wound over the floating stages front the wharf into the hold of the vessel. The machine by which this was done re-

it passed, while the usual apparatus was employed to test the integrity of the conducting wire. This test, however, would private, and none but those actually cononly show when the conductor was severed ; and not until the time for its committal to the deep arrives will it be seen whether it has been so attenuated in certain portions as to part during the process of paying out. From the small machine on deck it was wound at once to the hold, where it lay in one stupendous solid coil 15 feet in diameter, and nearly 14 feet high. It was beautifully arranged here, laid coil over coil with the most perfect accuracy, and every guard against a " kink" or fault occurring There is the fogs, precaution taken to in the paying out. Its being ranged in one mass will much facilitate the operation of submerging. We have before explained how the cable was coated with closely-woven spiral wires, to prevent damage to the core in paying out ; but, in consequence of the two halves having been made at different places þÿ one at Birkenhead, by Messrs. Newall, and the other at Greenwich, by Glasse and Elliot þÿ the twist of the spiral wires of the Birkenhead half is in the opposite direction to the twist of the wires in the half made at Greenwich. Thus, when joined in the centre of the Atlantic, they will form a right hand and a left hand screw, and the tendency of each will be to assist the other to untwist, and expose the core. By attaching a solid weight to the centre joining it is hoped this difficulty and danger

may be overcome. We shall hereafter describe the process of paying out the cable. (Continued ) APPROXIMATIVE ESTIMATION OP THE VALUE OF MANURES In consequence of the variation in the composition of manure, and the constant adulterations practised by unprincipled dealers, it is a matter of considerable imporiance to the farmer to be able in an easy manner to obtain an approximative value of any manure which he may have subjected to analysis; and we subjoin a mode of valuation, the use of which will at least save him from the gross imposition to which he is at present subjected. The substances which analysis and practice have proved to be most efficient as manuring principles are phosphates, and nitrogen in any of its forms. A few isolated experiments prove potash to be of some value in one or two crops; but, as this substance can readily be bought in a state of tolerable purity as sulphate or muriate of potash, and as it is not generally found in compounded manures, we shall not give this any agricultural value, further than as comprised under the term of alkaline salts. Silica, under any of its forms, has not yet been proved to have any agricultural value ; and carbonate of lime (chalk) is in most instances a s rinus detriment to a manure, though useful on the large scale, wheu used per acre by tons at a time From a careful comparison of numerous analyses of manure with the value of the substances therein contained, we have been led to adopt the following prices as giving the nearest approximative value of the several manuring

Now, gentlemen, as 1 have before intimated, it is very difficult to compress all the matters which 1 desired to bring before you within the compass of one brief lecture. lean only say, in conclusion, that 1 am exceedingly obliged to you for the very kind And attentive manner in which you have received my remarks this evening, and that if after 1 have sat down, there should be any points on which you wish to obtain from me additional information, I shall be very happy, if possible, to afford it (cheers). The Chairman said he concurred in almost everything the lecturer had said. Ho sawconsiderable doubt depicted in the countenances of some gentlemen present while Mr. Nesbit was explaining the system of cutting clover twice and relying on the decay of the cloverroots for manure for a wheat-crop ; but he had himself said, in the presence of four or five persons whom he met this morning, and without knowing any opinion of Mr. Nesbit, nearly word for word wnat they had just heard on that subject He had found that in other parts of the country clover was the crop that preceded wheat ; and any one who would take the trouble to examine carefully when lie ploughed up clover, would perceive that the abundance and size of the roots were likely, when in process of decay, to afford to the wheat-crop a large quantity of valuable manure. The only question was, whether the

moisture of their climate nught not prevent the roots of clover from producing the same effect that they produced in other parts of the couutry Hear, hear.- Of that he could form no opinion. Dr. Derby Pearse said he wished to put a question to Mr. Nesbit. He wished to know what was the nature of carboliu-acid þÿ au acid mentioned in a pamphlet which he met with, the other day, "On the preservation of natur.,1 manures," by Alexander M'Dougall, who spoke of it as one of two acids, the oilier being sulphurous acid, and the bases magnesia and lime. Oil tint seeing the term "carbolic" be was disposed to conclude that it was a misprint; but it afterwards appeared that that was not the case It was stated that by the agency of this compouu 1 the noxious p inciples were removed, and the valuable ones preserved it was of course i ery important to obtain a perfect deodorizer, winch this agent appea ed to be, while its value was alleged to he increased by its not ex rting any detrimental action upon those el ments which farmers wished to pieserve. He might thus illustrate the benefit to be derived from a good deodorizer. A stallfed cow would void 15 0001 bs, of urine in a year, which would yield 240lbs of ammonia, in addition to the phosphates of the urine and all the other excrements. Of this 240lbs. of ammonia no less tli ,n 162lbs. were annually lost by the ordina y mode of treatment, or rather neglect, ot the urine Ammonia could not be purchased by the. farmer for less than 6d. per lb. 162lbs of ammonia at 6d was 81s.,

the annual value per head for stall-fed cattle of the manure 1 st troin the urine alone. '1 lie loss on the other excrements was proportionably great. This 81s. worth of ammonia was dissipated in the air, generating disease and impoverishing the soil. Mr. Nesbit said there certainly was 6uch a substance as carbolic acid His opinion of it was, that however valuable it might prove when used on a small scale, it was utterly impossible to use such a substance or combination on a large scale It might be employed, perhaps, with advantage in a gentleman's stable ; but he would not recommend Cornish farmers to res it to it for the purpose of arresting the ammonia in their dung, for the simple reason that the quantity which would be required could not be produced. Moreover, every fanner had at his own door the most valuable of nil deodorizers, in the shape of common earth. When the dead were buried out of their sight, all the products of decomposition were absorbed by the earth; and when there was such a ready resource at hand lor arresting the odours emitted by manures, he could not advise them to have recourse to any expensive means of securing the same object, even if it were available to a sufficient extent

Mr. It. Wise was desirous of putting to Mr. Nesbit a question having reference to his remarks on the subject of clover. In that neighbourhood it was the practice to eat down clover; and there was, he believed, a clause in a 1 the leases prohibiting the cutting of clover twice in succession He would be glad to hear from Mr. Nesbit whether or not his remarks were applicable to the laying down clover for two years. Mi . Nesbit said he knew that was a question which admitted of a great deal of argument. He was aware of the practice of laying down clover for two years. But they lived in too enlightened tiin s to follow the practice of their ancestors, merely because it was their practice; circumstances might have arisen which required that they should deviate from it. For example, their ancestors did not use artificial manures to stimulate the growth of their crops; and hence, in their wisdom, they laid down the ground for a certain number of years, in order that vegetable matter might accumulate there It was in this way that he ac counted for the prevalence in that county of the practice of laying down seeds for two or three years. He thought it would be worth while to ascertain by experiment whether one year would not suffice; whether, by means of a sort of modification of the four-course rotation, they might, in four years, obtuin a better return than they had done under the present system. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. E. Phillpotts observed that the agriculturists of that neighbourhood were in

the habit of seeding out, not only with clover, but also with some of the other grasses. He would bo glad to know whether or not that practice interfered with the application of the principle laid down by the lecturer. Mr. Nesbit said, the grasses generally did not enter so largely into the question as clover. He had been speaking more particularly of cluver. The grasses were not of the same race as clover ; and, not having so large an amount of roots, did not follow exactly the same rule. When they were laying down a regular pasture, of which clover would form only a small portion, the principle which he had laid down was not applicable to quite the same extent that it was in the case which he had supposed; but still it was applicable to this extent, that it would not answer to feed with cl >ver unless they were laying down the land for a great number of years, and even then it would be better to let the clover grow for a certain time than to let it at all be fed oil' as it was produced. They could keep a much larger quantity of animals by that means, than b\ allowing the stook unlimited access to tin pasture. The. Chairman said, a gentleman had re marked that he thought the leases in thai neighbourhood contained a clause which pro hibited the cutting of clover twice. The gen tleman was quite right ; such a clause was always inserted, and it was important to bear that in mind in discussing this question The Rev. Mr. May thought it might, in some cases, be desirable to feed sheep on

half the crop, and to cut and plough-in the other half. Mr. Nesbit said, what he had been advo eating was, the allowing the clover to he fully developed belbre it was either fed off or cut. To cut it completely, and then allow it to develop again, would certainly be preferable to continuous feeding; but by ploughing in both th,: top and the bottom growth they would of course obtain the greatest result in the after crop. The best course to he pursued depended to a great extent on the amouut of vegetable matter in the soil. The plan of letting clover acquire very largo roots might not always answer on some peculiar descriptions of light land, a certain mechanical compre-sed condi tion of the soil being required in exceptional cases He knew that Mr. Hudson, of Oastloacre, found that it would not do for him, iD certain cases, to cut clover twice, because his land was too light.
