COMMUNICATION. For the 8t. Croix Avis. Mr. Editor ! Now that you are calling the attention of I your readers to a lecture on Agricultural Chemistry, 1 think it on few brief remarks a fit opportunity to offer a the present state of things connected with the Agricultural prospects of the Island It is an established and well known fact, that St. Croix is the only Sugar-producing Colony in the West Indies, which, in proportion to its size and resources, is incapable of the cause assigned for its incapacity is þÿ competing with any of the other Islands, scarci- and ty of labour. Although the insufficiency of labour is, without doubt, a great obstacle to the advancement of the Agricultural condition of the Island, it is not the greatest. There are many Estates in this Island, on each of which there is a sufficient quantity of labour for its proper cultivation, but in many instances that labour is misapplied, besides which, the labourers do not perform much more than half the quantity of work they ought to, andw perform, and every planter is well aware that no trifling loss is sustained by an injudicious application of labour ; on such Estates then, an additional supply would not only be unnecessary, but would increase the annual expenses, without resulting in any benefit to the property. With regard to those Estates which have not a sufficient it may be judiciously applied, yet quantity of labour at their command, the although amount j of work performed, is not what it should be, and as long as the present system of compel-

ling the l ibourer to work 9 hours daily, exists, no one need look for brighter prospects. One of the greatest misfortunes which has befallen the country, is the abolition of task work ; no blame whatever can be attached to the Government, as they certainly performed their part by allowing it to be tried and leaving the question to bo finally sc tied amongst the Planters themselves. Now ii has been admitted, even by its opponents, that the task system is an excellent one, but that the manner in which it was wrought would have resulted in the ruin of the country ; No one can deny that the system was most shamefully abused, and why 1 because the Managers on . some of the Estates where it had been introduced in order to attach the labourers to the Estate and induce others to seek for employment there in October, apportioned to each labourer an insufficient quantity of work which could be performed in 3 or 4 hours ; a fact which is too well known to he refuted ; the defect therefore, lay, not in the system itself, but in its application A much better remedy could have been found for its abuse, than its totd abolition; would the laws of a land be repealed because they weie bauly administered I assuredly not, competent persons would be appointed to administer them ; It would have been an easy matter for the Administrators of those Estates, ori which the system was so shamefully abused, to have prohibited their Managers, on pain of dismissal, from giving task work, until such

time, as they could prove to the satisfaction of their employers that the quantity of work they assigned to the labourers, would accrue to the benefit of the property. It is, 1 think, unfair, that those who know how to benefit by the system, should be prevented from cultivating their properties as economically as possible, because their neighbours abuse the means by which such an advantage may be gained. I do not hesitate to assert, that task work judiciously carried out, would be tbe salvation of St. Croix, and I am confident, in fact I know that labourers from some of the English Islands could be induced to corne here, provided they are allowed to work by task, as they will not work otherwise ; and I would here remind those who are opposed to task work, that the thriving condi tion of most of the Windward Islands, is to be attributed mainly to the adoption of the system, not, as some Planters here assert, to more favourable weather, for such an idea is only imaginary ; if therefore, task work can be so successfully carried on in the other Islands, why can it not be done here ? it only requires perseverance, and patience; judgment it does not require, more than what every Manager ought to possess who knows any thing of his business.

$ lu Cr, ft 0 I) X A V7 (I $U Suppose, for instance, a labourer is in the habit of weeding 3 or 4 rows of a cane field daily ; give him 5 or 6 rows for a task and see that it is proper'y done, when he has finished ; and so in proportion with other work ; any one that will take ti e trouble to make a calculation will see what advantage is gained. It is true, that tbe. labourers, in some instances, will lurry through the work and perform it badly, >ut the Manager has only to in-ist on its beiig honestly performed, and on no account to pay them their wages until he is satisfied that it is properly done. As long as tie present system exists, we need not expect a change for the better ; each succeeding year will bring with it a cry for "more labour" "more rain" þÿand, what is becoming yearly of more þÿimportance, a higher premium for labour, in the shape of bribery, which latter evil could be obviated by encouraging Immig ation. 1 have offered these few v marks in a friendly spirit, as I know there are many who will admit their truth, and I sincerely hope that the ,day is not far di-tant when a change will but effected, so as to enable this fast-declining be beautiful Island, to be placed in competition with others An Agriculturist.

STORE-BREAKING. On Monday night last a most daring theft was perpetrated by entering the stores from the root of Messrs. Crawford, Ure & Co. The manner of entering may be d. serving ot explanation, þÿ there being tiro roofs to the store, the first or under one being flat with layers of brick for a covering, and the second a pitched wooden roof with tiles above. In the upper roof there is at the south end a door, which not being the most secure was easily entered, when the malefactors must have proceeded to remove the bricks, and lastly descend into the store. From this it will be seen that the shelter of the upper roof afforded them all confidence whilst working at the under one. The spoils, from all that can be missed,

consisted in carrying to the wharf the Iron Sale, and 1. ere trom appearances smashing in tin- lid villi a stone, þÿ the contents, some two hundred dollars, being carried oil' and the broken sate thrown into the sea. However, this is not the worst feature of the case, for a fur more (earful deed was attempted, by trying with certain matter collected to ignite the place, which most fortunately did not succeed. We trust that this circumstance will afford others the opportunity of experiencing the fallacy oi relying 011 cast iron safes as a means of security, tor to use the remark we once heard u Smith make, it is enough to shew them a sledge or a stone to make them crumble beiore you. They are for all purposes of use not unlike Peter Pindar's Razors, with this exception, that those who buy them are more effectually shaved than Peter's razor ever pretended to do. We have so frequently attempted to hold up the picture of insecurity to property here alter night tall, that to advert to it again seems very much like relating the fable of the wolf, only that we do not affect to create a false alarm, as our cry is generally heard after there is an undeniable proof that the wolf has been and left behind marks of his depredations in testimony of what we state. It may, however, in the sequel so happen that the anology between our remarks and the liible will be that we have only been crying wolf at the trespasses of a few cubs, but that we may have to deplore the coming some day of a great
powerful wolf, whose acts may plunge the whole community in sorrow for another generation. Are u>e then never to have some means of protecting property after night

Mr. Nesbit said he considered Liebig's suggestion as to the use of oil of vitriol, in dissolving a portion of the bones, one of the greatest hints ever thrown out to practical agriculturists. THE GUANO CLAIM ON MONAGAS, &c., <fcc. Washington, August 10, 1857. The parties holding certain claims upon the government of Venezuela have been for some time urging the State Department to take such action in the matter as would bring President Monagas to the shelling Some of them out point, but without success thus far. The history of the matter is briefly as follows : þÿ A few years since there was quite a rage among our enterprising speculators of the North and East to fit out small expeditions to the Carribean Sea for the purpose of bringing away the surplus deposits of phoson tho numerous uninhabited cays and islets of that region, and which, after being

T, < & 0 I & V I: ground to powder, was sold in th mark under the different names of Mexican gu.iiio. South American guano, &c. In pursuit of this article every approachable cay lias been ransacked and its surface coating boated off. The business itself bus not proved a very profitable one, for the cost of outfit of the expeditions and the expense of collecting, &e., have more than balanced the proceeds, and it is said that no one of the many who engaged in the business lias made money at it. Among these active speculators was Philo S. Shelton, of Boston. The captain of a schooner fitted out by him landed on Aves or Bird Island, in the Carribean Sea, and, alter a cursory examination, supposed the deposit to be many thousand tons. He took possession of it, and reported to Mr. Slielton. This gentleman immediately fitted out several vessels, and sent them with picks, shovels and spades, to bring away the guano. But some title was wanted to the island, so that possession of it could be held against intruders, arid an agent was sent to Venezuela, whether by Mr. Shelton or other parties is not clear, to obtain one from that government. Venezuela had not the shadow ot a claim to the sovereignty of Aves Island, for it lies several hundred miles from her shores, and about sixty west from the French island of Guadeloupe. A title from her, however, would serve all necessary purposes, and that was enough. Certain Philadelphia lawyers, however, had heard that there was a speculation on foot, and they put in for it, too. A Mr.

Wallace was sent by them to Caucus to get the grant at any price. In Venezuela Mr. Wallace assumed the style of a great capitalist and gran senor, and his niagnifi cent offers soon left all others in the shade. A bargain was struck with Monugus for an exclusive privilege of working all the guano islands on the coast of Venezuela, including Aves or Bird Island. For this privilege the Philadelphia Guatio Company agreed to pay 8150,000 in cash, and give to Mouagas a royalty of five dollars per ton of guano procured, besides a one-third share of the profits of the enterprise. Wallace paid the S150,000 by drafts on Philadelphia, and Monagas sent a small schooner-of-war to Aves Island, and drove away Shelton's half-dozen of vessels and squad of men. When Wallace got home the Philadelphia Guano Company was organized with a great flourish, the stock was put into the market, and the bills in favor of President Monagas were ace >pted. A few vessels wore sent to Aves Island, and soon brought away what phosphate of lime was found there, which turned out to be a very small quantity after all. Other islands included in the grant were sublet to John E. Gowan, now gone to Sebastopol to raise the sunken Russian ships, but they soon THE VENEZUELAN þÿDIFFICULTY gave out also. Having got all that was to be found, the Philadelphia Company blew up, and President Monagas' bills returned unpaid. Air. Shelton's friends took hold of the presumptive claims against Venezuela for dispossession Aves Islands, and employe ! of

Mr. Sandford, late Secretary of Ligation at Paris, to prosecute the claim at Caracas. came here and got Marcv to instruct Mr. Eames, our Minister at Venezuela, to push the subject, and ever since then they have been pestering Congress, bothering the Secretary of State, publishing pamphlets, and getting newspaper correspondents to write about their great, claim against Monagas' government. Monagas, however, felt that he had been phate of lime salts that were to be found cheated all round, and asserted roundly that the whole atfair was nothing but a Yankee trick to get money out of him.

Mi n oes wanted to come home to trig wh els of applicants for his post, and Inning got the necessary permis-ion for a temporary absence, wrote a valiant letter to the Venezuelian government about the affair, thinking, no doubt, that zeal in favor of an American claim would be a great card for him to play here. But the Minister and the friends of Mr. Shelton, who have clubbed to prosecute a big claim in the hope to get something, find that Gen. Cass is too wary to be drawn into it as Marcy had been, the whole thing having a vast deal of making up in it. There is little doubt, however, that if Air. Shelton's creditors will reduce their demands within the bounds of reason, the government will press their claim in a proper way. He certainly held certain possessory rights, of which he was unjustly deprived, but not to the extent they pretend to demand. Eames has made himself simply ridiculous in the course he has taken, and it is not improbable that a new Minister may be sent to Caracas.
(From the London Times, Aug. 14.) LORD RAGLAN AND THE ENGLISH ALLIANCE.

In the Paris press the paper that discusses English questions with the greatest fairness, temper, and judgment is unquestionably the Republican Steele. In its criticisms there is no rancour, no petty spite, and in its censure, when it thinks proper to employ censure, it speaks of England as a great and free nation ought to be spoken of. Our institutions, though monarchical, are discussed by the Republican organ with impartiality. Our prejudices and our faults are Jenderly dealt with, and our virtues frankly done justice, to. One of the editors of the Steele, M. H. La Marclic, whose remarkable articles on foreign policy during the Russian war were much admired, has published a work entitled L' Europe et lu Hume, in which the excellent qualities I have just alluded to appear in every page. M. La Marche is a veteran of the Empire and a thorough Frenchman, but his predilections for his own country have not prevented him from doing justice to those whom he met þÿ foe in times now, happily, gone by and as a gone by, it is to be hoped, for ever. Alluding to the Generals who commanded the allied forces iu the Crimea, it is pleasing to hear an old soldier of the First Napoleon thus speak of the English General whom, in other days, he may have met as a foe in the Peninsula: þÿ " If it can be said of any man that he knew not what fear was, that man was Lord Raglan. His life did not weigh a scruple when duty was concerned. Full of instruction, affable without familiarity, forgetful of his own merits and bis

own services that ho might bring forward those of others, ho stands forth as a model of military virtue. When in front of any position which could be taken by open attack he never hesitated, and his dispositions were made with promptitude and method But when the act was to he preceded by the labours of special arms of the service, the noble Lord too modestly abdicated the authority which his geueral experience of war gave him Ever ready, ever disposed to act against all that could be overthrown by sheer gallantry, ho perhaps was deficient in initiative. Lord Raglan was a hero, but lie was not a captain 1 know that I speak of a noble old man, who is destined to die in a few months, perhaps, of the privations he has voluntarily imposed on himself during the winter þÿ that ho, a Peer of Great Britain, should not be exempted from suffe lngs in the midst of his soldiers who suffered cold and hunger, þÿ but wo must not speak of an adversary, or wo most say of him what we believe to be the truth. I will say, then, that it is almost incomprehensible that Lord Raglan, who went through all the campaigns of the Written before Lord Kaglan'n death

Peninsula side by side with the Duke of Wellington, should have allowed his army to tall into complete confusion in its administration, with the example of a General-in-Chief before him, his Mentor and his friend, and who owes, perhaps, his greatest success to the activity, to the real talent, with which he directed and always controlled his military administration. The French lost Spain because, instead ot liberally paying for all they wanted for consumption, they established that war ought to support war, and thus raised against themselves two sorts of interests, and rushed without precaution through masters, and applying to the word administra every sort of obstacle, laughiug at their ' quartertion' an epithet by no means flattering. Now see the change in human affairs. It is the Eng lish who perish in the Crimea for want of a properly organized administration, and it is the French who resist, thanks to the carefulness of their administration, and who fraternally aid their allies." Alluding to the alliance, he says : "When I speak of the English alliance I do not mean simply a Government giving its baud to a Government. I understand a people giving its arms to a people þÿ a democracy to a democracy. The English dewooracy has not the sauio forms nor all tho same instincts as ours. It pear prefers liberty to equality ; unity does in external to it absolutely necessary except not apaction. The necessity which the two nations experience agree to in their march is the more

goal by powerful inasmuch as they different roads. The proceed to which mistrust the same the English alliance inspired, and which it still inspires, arises from a perfect anachronism. Old England is dead, and it is she we might still mistrust. There have been þÿ no doubt there are, and always will be þÿ certain difficulties in the relations existing between these two great nations. But what alliance between equals has ever been without difficulties ? lhe war in the East having to be settled by a continental action, the first part belonged to France, however great wore the maritime efforts of England. Peace was obtained by a victory in which the English bore a fine and noble part, but which, in the eyes of the world, was a French victory. England bore with the exigencies and susceptibilities ol France in the execution of the treaty ot the 3 J t li of March, which France would have shown had the peace been obtained by the capture of Cronstadt, where our army bad the part which the English army filled at tho Malakhoff. Succeptibilities which would be intolerable iu an individual are respectable in a great nation. Let us not be so unjust as to complain that the English experience sentiments which we should experience in their place. Tho Mini ter who directs the policy of' Great Britain signed the treaty of the loth July, 1840. He maintained on the subject of the Spanish marriages a controversy which partook of the hatred ot ancient times. That was an accident arising from a Minister

having lived sufficiently long and in a spirit sufficiently progressive to enable him to acknowledge &Dd repair his errors. Did not Lord Aberdeen, who could not entirely divest himself of tho old man, fall from power? We might feel that we had a right not to forget the affair of Egypt, nor that of Pritchard, nor that of the right of search, and should we expect that England would forget that in the year 1852 the idea of an invasion occupied every mind in France ? Should malice therefore be established as a special privilege for our country ? People do not fight nor even quarrel any longer, thank God, except for interests more or less conformable to reason. Well, there are no more interests necessarily hostile between France aud England. VVe have no longer any colonies which England can envy us except Algeria, which we are too well able to defend for anybody to eudeavour to take from us. England, moreover, has completely changed her colouial system. All her possessions beyond the seas have obtained free trade, and almost all are invested with the right of self-government under the suzerainele rather than the sovereignty of the mother country. A new maritime law of nations secures the commerce of the weak from the attacks of the strong. The agreement concluded on maritime questions is drawD up in the terms which France never ceased to demand. Is it, then, on the continent that England should sause us uneasiness ? We do not believe that England wishes for all that we wish in Germany
and in Italy, but she wishes for many things there for which we ourselves wish. There is

A Voter has shown some interest in the welfare of this community so far as to propose, that the three gentlemen named be elected as members of the Colonial Council. A non-voter would first refer to your editorial remark in your paper of Tuesday the 15th inst., and next observe, that although Messrs. Rothe and Hawley are undoubtedly qualified gentlemen, yet the former has publicly once before objected to be voted for ; and as regards the latter, one cannot for a moment suppose that he would accept the membership as his time may be far better applied to the fulfillment of the manifold clerical duties that call for an active, energetic, assiduous and persevering attendance. X.

We would not make any remarks on the above communication did we not think that the reference to our editorial of the 15th inst., might lead to a misunderstanding of our views. Our opinion on the causes why the Colonial Council has passed so few measures b neficial to the public may be stated in a few words þÿ the Government -element has been too strong. If the public elect the Odicials of the Island as their representatives, we must expect that very little difference of views will be manifested in the discussions in that Council. Sufficient power to sustain the Government will, we think, be found in the selection of Officials as Crown Members; especially as the whole duty of the Council amounts to but an advice, which may or r uy not be taken, Wc cannot agree with þÿ þÿX in his views as regards the two gentlemen proposed in the voting ticket. That Chamberlain Rothe signified his intention on the 1 4th August 1852, not to accept an election, is true enough ; but we have no right to suppose that his intentions are the same in 1857 As regards the clerical duties which þÿX thinks ought to prevent llev. Hawley from accepting a nomination as memb r for tliis district, we think his remarks tako on the form rather of an opposition than otherwiso. If Rev. þÿHawley sclerical duties did not prevent his accepting a Government nomination during the l ist Session, we cannot see why they should prevent him from accepting a nomination as representative fir this district Every man has his private duties to

perform, whether of a clerical or secular nature, and every man has also public duties to perform. Neither of these duties can he claim a right to neglect. If n ither of the three gentlemen, proposed in the voting ticket, intends to accept a nomination, if elected, we think he or they owe a duty to þÿ at once. Mr. Editor, I fully indorse the sentiments which you expressed some days ago in the Avis when noticing the app.oachu.g election of Three members for this Jurisdiction to serve in the Colonial Council, and 1 am induced to trouble you with a few observations relative to the same subject, iu consequence of learning that many voters have expressed their determination not to go to the Foil, alledging as their reason for doing so, that the Colonial Council although established now over four years had effected nothing beneficial for the Colony, but on the contrary, inst ad of passing useful measures to lessen the expcnces of the country or relieve the people of one single burden, they had continually increased Taxation ; and that it appeared no Bill emanating from those members who had been elected by the people weie allowed to pass, Government having the power to out vote them þÿ with many other remarks of the same tendency. Now, admitting the truth of all this, it does not appear to me a sensible or just excuse for any þÿmail renouncing s such an honorable and a valuable privilege. The Colonial Council no doubt has disappointed the hopes and expectations generally formed of it on its first institution, but iu this there is no just ground for despairing of its eventually

becoming a valuable institution þÿ Rome was not built in a day and what the to the Bland. Colonial Council may become hereafter greatly depends upon the voters themselves. þÿ Return right men and þÿyou have ll right þÿineisureV The law does not confer the 1 ig lit of Franchise upon any man for his own personal behoof, but for the general good, and lie who is posses-ed of such a right is bound by the obligations of duty which he owes to the community of which he forms a part, to exercise the privilege, lie is thereby entitled, to the best of his judgment in voting for such men 11s can have no other interest to serve than that of the general good, and whose abilities fit them for such a position. The Ticket presented by a voter for accept nnce in your last paper is about as good a selection perhaps as can be made, and I would advise all to vote for it. But if another should be decided upon which may be considered better, let votes be concentrated and carry it, and let no heed be paid to those about the Galleries who, in order to split up votes, and to curry favor with persons who they consider greater than themselves, would have rnen s lected, who, by reason of personal interest, or the want of capacity, are unsuitable. Let voters use their own unbiased judgment. Another Voter. Christiansted 21st September 1857.

The bone of contention is the steamer Cagliari and the Sardinian passengers who were captured on board of her. Piedmont insists that ship and prisoners should at once be given up, and, certainly, it the published accounts be strictly correct of the manner in which the Cagliari was obtained possession of by the Mazziniaim, t he persistence is reasonable and should be complied with. But Naples is said to have replied to the demand by an insinuation that the Piedmontese Government might have done more than it did to prevent the recent revolutionary attempts in Italy. Thus, at least, it has been stated in certain foreign papers. 1 am assured that the King of Sardinia is disposed to carry matters with a high hand, and lie is said to be determined, if Naples refuses his request, not only to withdraw his Anibassa lor, but also to declare war. One has difficulty in believing that he would so promptly adopt so strong a measure. I need hardly point out that, if he did, the affair would lie most serious, and might very probably be fatal to the peace of Europe. Austria would at once side with Naples. Austria, however, is by no means desirous of seeing things come to such a pass, and is doing her utmost to make up the quarrel. The latest accounts received in Paris are a shade more favourable than

the preceding ones to a peaceful settlement of the quarrel, but there still are grounds for some little þÿuneasiness. Later intelligence says that the Neapolitan Government is induced to pause at, the idea of breaking oft' diplomatic ralations, assumes a more reasonable tone, and promises to bring its inquiries to a close within a short and stated time. From the New York Tribune. THE SCIENTIFIC CONGRESS. The eleventh meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, olosed its seven days Session on Wednesday of last week, in Montreal. The attendance was considerably larger than at Albany last year; nearly 500 members registered their names. The Scientific results attained were not so great as those of last year ; several of the most prominent members of the Association were uuable to attend. Perhaps the most striking contribution was the discovery of Prof. Peirce, that the principal lines of separation between land and water were arcs of great circles tangent to the polar circles. This will be rendered beautifully apparent by bringing the polar circles of a three horizon and revolving it. Only globe to the considerable shore-lines are exceptions, and two of (hose þÿ the northern line of South America and the range of islands of the Pacific are perpendicular þÿ to these tangents. When the sun is in the tropics, and it is very nearly for half the year, these lines are the limits between night and day; they are the lines of cotemporaneous sunset and sunrise. While the crust of the molten earth was just becoming solid, therefore þÿ when it was first freezing over þÿ the heat of the þÿsun r s ays on one side of these lines and the cold of night on the other would produce lines of cleavage, and when the world had cooled and shrunk so much as to be too small for its rock envelope, and begun to wrinkle it into mountains and valleys, they would follow these natural cleavages ; some

would be the bottom of the oceans and others the ridges of the continents. So we have to throw away the suppositions of the early geologists that the beds of the present oceans were once continents, and that the present continents were once oceans; and come to the belief that the grand features of the earth were determined in its original cooling. This is a result toward which the labors of geologists for several years have been tending. Mr. Ramsay, the Director of the Geological Survey of Great Britain, who was sent over as a delegate from the London Geological Society, sustained this view þÿ that the geological growth which we observe, has gone ou in past periods in much the same way as it is going on now. He showed from the number of animals which have survived all the great changes, that the6e changes must have been gentle and gradual ; such in fact as we see now in the subsidence of our Jersey coast, which Prof. Cook, of that State, showed pretty conclusively to be going down at the rate < f some twenty inches a century. The contributions ol Prof. Hall, of New-York, who traced the vety gradual growth of the American continent, and pointed out several formations which go to till up supposed gaps in our rock systems, had the same general tendencies. Prof. Hall thinks that tho Alleghanies were produced by deposits from a stream similar to the present Gulf Stream, which flowed down from the not th-east. He showed that the original deposits, thirty thousaud feet thick, must have been immensely worn away to

reduce these mountains to their present height, and that instead of being lines of elevation, they were in fact, lines of exoessive denudation, lie thinks also, that we have nowhere any evidence of a primary igneous nucleus on which the stratified rocks have been deposited, but that the so-oalled igneous rocks were deposited in tho same sober way as the rest, and owe their igueous appearance to metamorphic action. (From the Colonial .Standard, and Jamaica Despatch PATENT SLIP. Improvements advance in Jamaica by very slow gradations. It is now something like two years since an individual in our community, who, not expecting to live for ever, yet possessing that spirit of true patriotism which is content to lay the foundations of great and useful works, even though posterity should reap the fruits of present enterprise, suggested the expediency of rivalling St. Thomas in the estimation of the Royal Mail Steam Packet this port into a harbour of refuge for the Company, and at the same time of erecting this be I shipping of this quarter of the globe, by in procuring the erection in our harbour of i the machinery necessary for hauling-up and repairing vessels of the largest class. The Patent þÿSlip project has been, þÿ ever since, a joke in the hands of those who would designate those floating improvements which are supposed especially to characterise Jamaica. If this was not absolutely a þÿ castle in the þÿair, it was assumed at least to be not a fabric on the water; and so our friend of the Daily Advertiser, when he desired facetiously to conceptions, has þÿ been accustomed to describe them as patent slips.'' It is pleasant to find that, although the project which we felt so much pleasure in supporting at the time has dormant, it has not in fact been sleeping. The parties who originated the proposition friend in Manchester, explaining the project I have at length made a considerable move towards its realisation. If results can be predicated from well founded premises, we

think we can say that þÿ is yet destined to be, anil that at no great distance of time. We may slate that, long ago, the gentlemen who took a leading part in the proposition when first mooted, placed themselves in communication with Messrs. Bell and Miller, of Glasgow, with the view of ascertaining the cost of the machinery and apparatus necessary to carry out the wishes of those who met together and resolved on the expediency of erecting a Patent Slip, or Floating Dock, in this harbour. The result of their application was a full and gineers explanatory letter from the which named above, of eminent en- we are happy to be able to furnish a summary.

The cost of rails, cradle, steam engine, traction rods, hydraulic purchase machinery (patented, but with a moderate royalof taking up vessels of 3,000 ions, will be from <£8,500 to £9,000 at the þÿship side. s This would include a fortyhorse-power condensing engine, and the weight of the whole for shipment would be about 560 tons. In addition to this a diving bell will be necessary, the cost of which will be about £320 þÿ its weight with accessories being about 12 tons. It will be necessary to send out a working engineer, and a shipwright to erect the machinery, and to lay the ways of the Slip. Their wages are estimated at a similar rate as the wages of engineers seufc from England to Jamaica to erect sugar machinery, and' may be easily settled here. As a local survey would be necessary before any particular spot is selected for the erection of the Slip, Messrs. Bell and Miller have proposed hat one of their firm should proceed to this country for the purpose of surveying and reporting upon the

addition of £100 tor his trouble, and in the event of the work being gone on with, a further and usual engineering charge of 5 per cent, on the cost of the works will be demanded. We have much pleasure in stating that in the course of a few hours a sum of £250 has been subscribed in this city for the purpose of obtaining this preliminary survey. This amount will be remitted by the present steamer, and before three months have passed over our heads we hope to be in a position to place before our readers a report of this survey, and an announcement that the Patent Slip is no longer to be an editorial myth. It is impossible to say beforehand what U'ill the positive effect upon trade in island of the erection of so important a machinery as that in contemplation this harbour. We have heard it said that St. Thomas owes much of its maritime importance to the fact of its possessing the ouly machinery of the kind in the West Indies. Yet the Slip at St. Thomas is a very small affair. No vessel drawing over 7 feet of water can be taken up by it. The machinery proposed to be erected here would take up the Atrato or the Nile (91). Its cost, exclusive of the purchase of land, labour, and machinery, would, in round numbers, be about £10,000 in Jamaica. Such a sum as that might be raised, with no great difficulty, we should imagine, among ourselves. The further expences for material þÿ stone, principally þÿ and labour would have to be met by further subscriptions ; aided, however, as we should hope

apparently laid it would be, by the public. The Penitentiary could supply both the stone and the labour; and, if a pecuniary return were to be exacted by the Legislature, it might be estimated by an annual percentage on the value of the labour employed, to be a The Patent þÿSlip charge for a given number of years on the profits of the Slip. Assuming, however, that a work of this nature will influence as it may be expected to do the trade of this port, and thus act in a highly beneficial manner on the public revenue, it would be scarcely too much to expect that the assistance of the Penitentiary should be gratuitously supplied. In such a case, the work might be considered already in a fair way to completion. PIEDMONT. The Opinione , of Turin, gives an account of the reception, at Genoa, of the splendid piece of ordnance sent by the citizens of Boston to the people of Piedmont for the walls of Alessandria. General Durando commandant of the division of Genoa, and the civic authorities proceeded in state to the gates of the port, where the gun was solemnly delivered to them. It was then conveyed to the Piazza Nuova, accompanied by a band of music and by a detachment of soldiers. It remained there until the Monday following, to be viewed by the population, and was then sent off to Turin.

A Cavalry Charge at Nusseerabad. So much doubt was there regarding the native troops at Nusseerabad, that a picket of the Bom bay Lancers þÿ who fortunately had not been taken away from the station þÿ mounted guard over the Bengal battery. On the 29th of May, at about four in the evening, the storm broke over that devoted station. It commenced by a rush of the mutineers to the guns ; there they soon overpowered the few gallant Lancers who were guarding them, and loading with canister, these men numbering upwards of 2000, awaited the deadly strife. And now ensued a passage of arms, which for brilliant gallantry, determined coolness, and devotion, stands, I think, as we hear it, uuequalled iu the annals of history The Bombay Lancers (Tst Light Cavalry), who for seven days had remained booted aud saddled iu expectation of such emergency, were mounted and formed up instantly. Officers fell in at the heads of their respective troops, the word was given to march, and with the chivalry of Knights Templars this brave body (the number short of 200) went forward to almost certain death. As they neared þÿ the cursed battery the word was given to þÿCharge. Regardless of the fearful leaden shower that instantly opened upon them, and the terrific gaps it occasioned in their serried rauks, each man from the colonel to the youngest trooper, emulating the deeds of their gallant European comrades at Balaklava, only pressed the more eagerly and determinedly forward. Through and through the mutiuous scoundrels did they ride, aud ouly desisted when the com-

manding officer, seeing the gr at loss they hod already sustained, and the woful inequality of the contending parties, sounded the recall, and directed the few men who remained to cover the retreat of the ladies and families from the station This they did, conducting them in safety to u village thirty miles distant, from whence the handful of men again issued aud succeeded iu capturing one of the guns In this gallant affair the regiment lost Captain Spottiswoode and Cornet Newberry, killed ; Colonel Penney died immediately after the action ; aud Capt. Hardy aud Lieutenant and Adjutant Loch wounded; the number of men killed is not known. It is impossible to overrate the confidence this gallant conduct of the Lancers lias created in all quarters. Nobody ever doubted that the Bombay troops were faithful and staunch to a man, and this is the most undeniable proof they could have of it.

T ,- c 0 I x A V I S , COMMUNICATION. To the Editor oj ih : St. Croix Avis. Sir, þÿ 1 enclose you an Extract from the St. Croix Agricultural Reporter of July 1853. It struck me when reading " Custodia's" sensible letter how vividly lie depicted what was foretold four years ago ; and howvery similar many of his remarks were to the article in question. 1 would observe, that the writer in the Reporter had just returned from a visit to Jamaica, and had there seen the ruinous consequences of the wilful competition and wantonand reckless behaviour of the planters, which proved not only fatal to themselves but drew into the general ruin and disorganization of that once beautiful Island, Merchants, Shopkeepers, and even the labourers themselves. Surely Sir it is high time for our magistrates to enforce the highest penally for such shameful proceedings as have lately taken place, for 1 have heard it said that some of the persons since their conviction have boasted that they would bribe in spite of the authorities. I remain, Sir, Your Obedt. Servt. "SCRUTATOR." St. Croix, loth Oct. 1857. (Extract from the Agricultural Reporter.) We have to regret much, that a certain degree ot apathy lias been more or less shown by the Members of the Agricultural Society, to contribute their quota towards tilling the columns of the Reporter. It may he remembered by tiiose who closely scrutinize ttie pages of our publication, that a great similarity lias prevailed in the subjects which the various writers have touched upon. But this was natural, as

the object to be gained by the Society and the Reporter was, to aid agriculture and to disseminate men's opinions on its various bran lies. However we do not think it out oi place to moot a question of the greatest importance to our ivosjus well us to rhe >vh m community, premising thai ai tb crops are, the inoi 11 1 it in y that same column., On t us p nut we Quartermaster, j believe every on w about to touch up . ... . sub- W ' ttt'O ject, one that has in d þÿ by persous ot all occupation , and of course discussed pro el von. We allude to that formidable subject of the "yearly contract." We do not intend to enter into all the arguments that have been raised as to its advantages or disadvantages. We profess to be as thoroughly philanthropic as the most frequent attendant of Exeter Hail ; but we must insist upon having an experience I which the votaries of that institution have ; what we wish to impress upon our readers is, the great and vital importance, for the future welfare of this colony, that this contract should be fairly carried out. We " fairly, ' for who that reads these pages, say does not know all the disagreements and the heart-burnings that take place during months of August and September! And it these contracts were fairly made , that is, it planters were to remain passive and quietly allow our to seek employment, instead of population labouring being sought for, would it not he advantageous to all? We have tree people to deal with. They can choose their own employers. No coer-

cion is used to keep them on the Estates on which they are residing; hut 011 the contrary, in many instances advantages and inducements are held out to the laborers to leave their original employ for another which is supposed to he more beneficial, and which in nine cases out of ten, neither proves to he of any remunerative results to the employer or employed. We would ask, what does all this tend to ? To

excite dissatisfaction and uneasiness to nine tenths of our population, and to cause a had feeling between neighbors, which as long as it exists must ultimately end in the ruin of every one. We say this without hesitation, for as sure as 1111 Estate is crippled by the want of labour, so sure are its neighbours destined to feel its influence. We know that the yearly contract is the mainstay of the prosperity of the whole colony þÿ then why, witlfour eyes open, seek to destroy its good effects by wilful corruption? It is a slow poison, hut a poison that will prove fatal to all in the end. The most ultra-philanthropist to the labourer of our colony must be convinced of tiiis, were he to weigh well all the advantages of the yearly contract with the reckless extravagance of daily labor. We see around us 111 the neighbouring colonies, the population retrograding in civilisation, diverging to their aboriginal state and becoming careless of the blessings that Providence lias placed in their way. We have no doubt that our ideas on this subject will be criticise! ' they may even he scoffed at, but we earnest, request our readers to reflect seriously on the consequences of a system as pernicious in its immediate effect as it will be ruinous in its ultimate result. The remedy is easy ; fairness and candour among the Planters would check all the evils. We have no wish for any combination of employers, far from it; we wish to see the labourer choose of his own free-will the Estate that lie or

she should select for their abode; hut u do thoroughly condemn a practice of cajolery and bribery that every one knows, takes place more or less throughout the Island. We have heard some people try to justify their conduct by appealing to conscientious motives of doing the best lor their employers' interest. But this is a. most shortsighted argument ; they forget that there is a future day, when those same employers will expect a return from " their properties, and they even forget more, Do unto others as you would they should do unto you." The very men who boast of conscientious motives to obtain labour, forget that they arc liurryingtheir neighborsand their own employers to an ultimate ruin wuich will eventually swallow up all the resources that a bountiful Nature lias thrown open to our industry.

public opinion in this capital. RUSSIA. A telegraphic dispatch, dated Konigsberg, Sept. 21st, says : þÿ "Letters received by a commercial house in this city troin Russia state that the commission lor the emancipation of the peasants the following resolutions : þÿ ' The adopted has einancipation is to take place at three successive periods ; one to be occupied with preparatory measures; the second with the executive measures; and the third with the definitive arrangements, to be confirmed by law. In a manifesto from the Emperor, the landowners will be invited to conic to an arrangement with their peasants relative tot lie emancipation of the latter. The contracts between the owners and the peasants must contain these three clauses: þÿ ' 1. The land appropriated to each peasant to be farmed on the payment of rent, must be sufficient for his existence and for that of

his family. 2. The peasants must undertake not to leave, at least for the present, the lands they now occupy. 3. The payment of the taxes due to the State must be guaranteed.' The other clauses of the arrangement are to be left to the free will ol the contracting parties." Accounts have been received from St. Petersburg that the Czar, before leaving his capital, approved of the draft ot the project for the partial abolition of serfdom. On his Majesty's return, it is added, this . al ter passing through the Senate will be project will receive his final sanction, and published as a law, to accompanied bya mation addressed proprietors ol serfs, in- proclaviting or more strictly speaking commanding them to enter into arrangements for the liberation with their serfs, whose total numbers, including their families, do not fall short of 10 millions. It is needless to say, that the project, if carried out, will greatly endear the Czar to the masses, and cause him to be regarded as their liberator and father.

The Moniteur da Senegal of the 11th ult. gives the following account of the hostilities between the French and the insurgent natives : þÿ " Al Hadji, the insurgent chief, Burgher Council's Secretary's Office, St. subjected by the French, 'went at the begin- in spite of the defeats to which he had been ning of June to blockade the fortified town of Medina, in which, in addition to the garrison, was a native population of 6,000 souls, favourable to the French. The object in view was to take the place by famine ; but, in addition, Al Hadji made frequent assaults on it, .which caused a loss on botK sides. The French Governor of Senegal having at length determined on going to the relief of the place, sent off a small force of 120 men (only 20 of them whites) in the Basilic steamer, and went himself at the head of 80 men. At Bakel, the Governor obtained the co-operation of about 40 laptots (native volunteers), and went up to Medina, where he arrived ou the 17th of July, and was shortly after joined by the Basilic. Alter burning down the abandoned village of Soutoukholle, he attacked the forces of Al Hadji, consisting chiefly of Toucouleurs, and after an engagement, or rather a succession of engagements, in which the Toncouleurs fought with savage energy, he drove them away, and relieved the town. The loss on the French side was five killed or wounded, and on that of the enemy 40 killed. The garrison, headed by the commander, M.Paul Holl, and all the population, went forth to meet the French, with

every demonstration of joy ; thev were in a frightful state from hunger and disease : the town, too, was dreadful from filth, and at the foot of the walls were between 300 and European Times." Whether the fault lies 400 dead bodies in a state of putrefaction. If the French had not arrived, the resistance could not have been much longer prolonged, as the inhabitants of the place had no more powder, and the garrison had only one or two charges for their muskets, and two for garding a Gentleman from this Island who their four pieces of cannon. Al Hadji havhappened to be in St. Thomas when the ing rallied his forces and received reinforce- Pluropean Mails arrived and applied at the ments, advanced to attack the town on the 23rd, but the governor went out to meet him with a part of his forces, and having fallen in with him in a ravine at about three quarters of a league from the place, on the road to Gondiourou, attacked him with impetuosity A sharp engagement ensued,

and the result was that the enemy were obliged to retire, leaving 50 dead on the ground, and having a great number wounded. The French, however, did not think it prudent to pursue them, but they captured a great number of oxen and other booty. It was reported that the Toucouieurs were abandoning Al Hadji, and that the latter, being greatly discouraged, contemplated retiring to Dinguirav, his own village, in the Fouta Dialon."

AUSTRIA. Advices from Vienna state that the reports that were current to the effect that the Austrian Government intended to raise a loan of 150,000,000 florins, and to issue Treasury Bills to the same amount, have been contradicted. A letter from Vienna, says: þÿ "The Concordat is beginning to hear fruit ; the Cardinal de Rauscher, Archbishop of Vienna, was sometime ago charged l»v the Holy See to visit the convents and monasteries of his diocease, and to re establish primitive discipline wherever it might he relaxed. Among the convents which first attracted the attention of the prelate was that of the Dominicans?, and in consequence of the report addressed by him to the Pope, he received directions to re-establish the rules of the order in all their original rigour. All the members of the convent except two, however, replied that they had made vows to observe the rules which were in force at the time of their en trance into the convent, hut not to accept reforms which might subsequently be introduced. The old monks moreover represented that it would he absolutely impossible for them to submit to the original order of tilings, as it prescribes that the monks shall rise several times in the course of the night to pray in the chapel and to perform other painful exercises. Reference has been made to Rome, and the general of the Dominicans directed that the convent should he dissolved, if all the monks would not accept the reform. The monks persisted in refusing, and all attempts at concilia-

tion having failed, the convent has been dissolved, and the monks have been sent to the convent ofMeissan.in Moravia. What is singular is, that Belgians and Italians are to he brought in to occupy the convent of the expelled Germans ; hut hrtw are they, with their foreign language, to preach, hear confession, and perform their other duties as ecclesiastics?"

SPAIN. The accounts and correspondence from Spain with respect to the Ministerial crisis are rather contradictory. Although it is said to be over, the Government of Marshal Narvaez has received a rude shock. There is reason to believe that the formation of a new Cabinet was offered to Beltran de Lis, who declined undertaking it. A letter of the 19th says that Concha will remain at Cuba, Lersundi as Minister of Marine, and that Narvaez's protege , Marfori, will be Intendant of the Palace. The papers make a confusion between Moyano, a member of the present Government, and Don Luis Mayans, a relation of the Palace favourite, and who has been spoken of in recent prof»osed t is announced that Mayans is about to combinations for a new Ministry, leave for Valencia. General Armero, another intriguer, is to go to his estate in Andalusia. These departures from Madrid and the appointment of Marfori (if realized) look as if Narvaez had prevailed over his Palace enomies ; but it is a dangerous thing for a Spanish Ministry when the struggle with the camariUat gets as far as this.

There is talk of an early convocation of the Cortes, and of a vi olent opposition in the Senate by Manuel Concha and the Vicalvarists. Official intelligence has been received of the acceptance by the Mexican Government of the proffered mediation of England and France in the quarrel between Mexico and Spain. The conference for the settlement of this matter is to be held in London. This will probably not be very pleasing to Spain, which would fain have had it in Madrid. The capital of one of the mediating nations is manifestly the most suitable place. It is not yet known who will be the Plenipotentiaries appointed, but it is presumed that Senor Latragua will represent Mexico, he being completely au courant of the affair, which he has followed from the commencement. The whole personel of the Mexican Legation at Madrid is now in Paris. ft

ITALY. The Monitors Toscano gives an account of the inauguration of the statue of the Immaculate Conception at Rome on the 8th. The Pope, attended by numerous prelates, proceeded in a procession to the Piazza di Spagna, where the column surmounted by the statue is situate, and was received with great honours by the Spanish Ambassador. The Pope then blessed the monument, and burnt incense around it, after which the Ave Maria Stella was sung, and the Papal benediction given to the people. The Pope afterwards admitted the Ambassador and his household to the honour of kissing his slipper.

ARTESIAN WELLS IN ZAHARA. The official report of General Desvaux on the Artesian borings executed in the Zahara of the Province of Constantine in 1856-7 has just been published by the Moniteur Algerien, and is not without interest. A civil engineer, a sergeant of Spahis, and a detachment of soldiers of the Foreign Legion suffice for the work, which commenced early in May, 1856, in an oasis of the Oued-Rir. This first essay was most successful. On the 19th of Juue a perfect river, yielding 4,010 quarts of water per minute, at a temperature of 21 degrees, hurst from the bowels of the earth. The joy of the Arabs was indescribable. The news of this miraculous gush of water, so precious in the desert, spread rapidly through the country. People came frotn afar to see the spring, to which the Marabouts, with solemn ceremonies, gave the name of the " Fountain of Peace." The soldiers who had wrought the seeming miracle returned to Biskra without a single sick man, although during the period of their labours the centigrade thermometer had often marked 46 degrees in ttfe shade. Two other borings were also successful, but the supply of water was much less received the name of " Fountain of the abundant þÿ the first of the two wells, which Benediction," yielding only 35 quarts a minute from a depth of 81 metres ; the second, 120 quarts at the depth of 58 metres. The gratitude of the Arabs knew no bounds, and they showed the most friendly feeling towards lived ment of soldiers, who the slender detach- among them

for weeks and months together, at long distances from the French garrisons. In the oasis of Sidi-Rached, which was totally unproductive for the want of water, an Artesian well, known as the "Fountain of Gratitude," yields at the depth of 54 metres no less than 4,300 quarts of water per minute. When the shouts of the soldiers announced the gush the Arabs sprang in crowds to the snot, laving themselves in the welcome abundance, into which mothers

? T « & ft ft li ft A « li S. dipped their children, while the old sheik fell upon his knees and wept, and returned thanks to Allah and the French. At Ouin Thiour a well, sunk to the depth of 170 metres, and yielding 180 quarts a-miuute, was at once taken as the centre of a settlement by a portion of a previously nomadic tribe. As soon as the water appeared they began the construction of a village and the plantation of 1,200 date trees, and entirely renounced their wandering existence. According to General Desvaux's report, these Artesian wells are likely to have a most important influence on Arab life, and greatly to subdue the roaming propensities of many of the tribes. þÿ London Times.

OUGHT A FELLOW TO MARRY ? In a restricted sense, the above question lias been brought of late very prominently under discussion, although interesting to a small portion of the community. Taken in its larger acceptation, there is no subject of inquiry that can be more momentous to mankind, inclusive of womankind, except the still more important problem of being or not being, mooted by Hamlet. If a fellow did not marry what would be the consequence to society ? Clearly society would cease to exist ; and therefore if society ought to exist, it is certain that a fellow ought to marry. The question may thus be settled in a general way, but because a fellow ought, in the abstract, to marry, it does not follow that he ought to marry under all circumstances. A fellow may be too old to marry ; he may also be too young to marry, notwithstanding that he may have arrived at what the law calls years of discretion, but which are years of indiscretion in a multitude, if not in the majority of instances. A fellow may be too great a fool to marry, at least to marry anybody but a woman of sufficient sense to be able to take care of herself and him too. Such a woman is not often to be bad, and she will not accept a fool for a husband, unless he is a very opulent one ; but a woman who would marry a fool for his money can have no heart in her bosom, whatever amount of head she may carry on her shoulders. A foolish fellow, who marries a heartless woman, will find that he has made himself a greater lool than Nature constitu-

ted him : that in ceasing to be a single fool he has become a double tool. A fellow may also be too wise to marry, too much disposed to act in all affairs according to the dictates of reason, by which proceeding he will, in all probability, displease and exasperate his wife. Perhaps the reason why the celebrated Xantippe was such a vixen, was because her husband, Socrates, was so great a philosopher. lie would act on rational principles; he would have this or that done, or else know the reason why, and would not be content with a woman's reason. Then lie had a habit of questioning people, and getting them to convict themselves of absurdity if they were in the wrong; a habit calculated to provoke almost any woman. Women do not like to be argued down ; cannot bear to have a thing beaten into their heads ; would as soon be physically thrashed ; and, if you attempt to convince them, they cry. Too wise a fellow admires scarcely anything; and a wife, to be pleased, must be admired; if she is not pleased, she will not please, will not make home happy ; such a fellow, therefore, ought not to marry. A too ideal, poetical, imaginative fellow, ought not to marry. Poets and men of genius, such as Shakspeaiv, Milton and Byron, have been, in marriage, very generally, unhappy fellows. A poet fancies that the delight which seems to radiate from his sweetheart's face will continue to gladden him all the days of his married life. Now, this fellow ought not to marry, for if he does he will he disappointed ; he will

then, probably, become morose and ill-treat his wife, lie should procure a good portrait of bis beloved instead of marrying her ; the portrait will keep and her face will not. Marriage is a line of life, a business ; and if a fellow would enter upon it, he ought not to bo above his business. lie ought to be þÿ not, indeed, as the common phrase goes, domesticated, because that lie cannot be till lie has had experience of domestic life; but lie ought to be prepared to be domesticated. Just as a fellow who goes for a soldier should be disposed not only to accept, but to welcome, the incidents, commonly considered hardships, of the camp

T, 3 i 0 r< & AVfiS. and of warfare, so ought a fellow who marries to be ready and willing, and, indeed, eager, to encounter the trials, not to say troubles, of the matrimonial state. Doctors, dry nurses, wet nurses, the thrush, vaccination, measles, are things and persons that he should take a certain pleasure in the idea of meeting and providing for. If a fellow feels in his own mind that these are matters which he would regard as annoyances and bores, then that fellow ought not to marry. The phenomena of teething ensue generally necessarily marriage on þÿ if marriage answers its ends þÿ and before a fellow marries he ought to assure himself that the noise made by an infant undergoing dentition, if not exactly musical and er bleven lsest ved Over-og Under-Retterne soothing to his cars, will not deprive him her paa de Dansk Vesrindiske Eilande of sleep, or, at least, not deprive him of patience, and so irritate him as to spoil his temper, and render him disagreeable to his wife. Every vocation has its toils, which are pleasures to those who follow it from love; so should it be with matrimony ; and a fellow ought not to marry except for love, or at, least with love. A fellow ought not to marry for money ; if he does, he will probably find out his mistake ; that is, lie will discover that, instead of taring sumptuously and gratuitously every day, he will be called upon to spend not only the income for which he married, but a great deal more ; that he will be in debt, so that, instead of bettering his circumstances :

by mercenary matrimony, he will find that 1 he has reduced his means to less than noth- ! ing. His wife's revenue, if not the whole j of her property, will all go, and he will have bills to pay besides, unless he resoliuely sets his face against excessive expenditure, and so disgusts the lady. 80 that a fellow not only ought not, but had better not, marry for money, mere money, notwithstanding what imbecile old men, and fast young ones, may say to the contrary. On the other hand, a fellow ought not to marry unless he believes that he can maintain his wife. lie has no right to inflict a relation, and probably a number of relations, on his parents, uncles, brothers and sisters. But bow much will suffice to maintain a wife and family 1 That depends. One lady cannot be happy without an opera box, another will be satisfied with a carriage, another will be content with a drawing-room, somewhat elegantly furnished, and a piano ; very many contrive to exist in the fruition of the moderate comforts and luxuries procurable for nine shillings a week. Ought a fellow then, to marry who has #io better maintenance to offer a wife and probable family than that derived from nine weekly, and perhaps precarious shillings ? Ought, in short, a poor fellow to marry? If poor fellows did not marry what should we do for cotton-spinners, for agricultural labourers, for mechanics in general, for costermongers, for cat's and dog's-meat, men, for common soldiers and sailors. Certainly, then, poor fellows ought

ro marry, if rich fellows ought to enjoy themselves ; and if a poor fellow has married and reared a family 011 some few shillings a week, and has not saved enough out ol his wages to live upon in his old age, it is not just that he should be subjected to the discipline of a workhouse in order to punish him for improvidence. Pauperism is a great social evil ; but there is a greater, which would be averted if fellows generally observed the rule which appears, with certain exceptions, to hold good þÿ the rule that a fellow ought to marry.

EXTRACT OF THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE BUR- GHER COUNCIL OF ST. CROIX. McXj L &1WL the Burgher Council held an ordinary session. Member Heilbuth absent. Following cases referred. Letters and communications from Government : Forwarding copies of alphabetical lists conformable to the law of 26th March 1862 11 concerning the Colonial Council. Forwarding list of arrears of taxes in Frederiksted for the year 1866 requesting that those paid be struck off; the lists rectified and returned. That the Commander of the Station at Kingshill has reported the death of a foal 17 months old, from the strangles. Approving of the Council's proposal to lend 8500 of the rumfuud to Mrs. Ann Ellis ; þÿ her bond being produced the amount was assigned. Letter from the Stadshauptman, stating in reply, that he had applied to a mercantile house at St. Thomas to learn, if sale could be found there for the old militia guns &c. still on hand, but was informed, that it could not be effected, especially as they are defective and of an old construction. He observes, that in 1855 a committee was appointed by the Government to examine all the arms and that this committee did condemn them all ; the leather trappings and accoutrements are of no value, and would only cause expense if sold at auction ; he proposes, that the arniB be sent to Copenhagen, where something may be had for them. Council resolved to adopt this proposal and requested the Stadshauptman to have all the arms selected, and as regards the

leather trappings &c., to have them sold when an auction at the military depot shall be kept. Representation to be made to Government. Memorial from planters Messrs. Newton, Mc'Caul, G. Mudie, C. Lucas, Christmas and Ratcliffe for themselves and in behalf of the other planters and absent proprietors, soliciting the Council to urge a decision on its representation to the Government of the 9th August 1856, and to cause all other necessary steps to be taken for furthering and bringing to a practical issue the question of the importation of free Africans. The Council resolved to forward a copy of the memorial to the Government and require information regarding the Council's representation of the 9th August 1856 on the question of immigration. Members Sarauw and Elliott produced two estimates, drawn up by A Ferris and A. Leidesdorff, of the cost of repairs required at the public school at Frederiksted, and promised at the next meeting to report on the said work and make their proposal. The Inspector of the rural schools Revd. Gardin was present, pursuant to an invitation from the Council, for the purpose of discussing the subject : in what manner the instruction in needle work may be pro- cured most economically. - Mr. Gardin observed, that as regards the schools at Easthill and Laval Ice, these being provided with dwellings, and as the number of children frequenting them is not reat, the salary for said instruction may be xed at $4 or 5 pr. month for each ; but as regards the other schools the greater
number of children frcquentingthem, makes it desirable to obtain the assistance of the female teacher in the general branches of instruction during the school hours, and

T, t II. ? U ft Y (i | that no qualified teacher can be hud for less than 86 per month. lie furthermore pointed out the necessity of erecting dwellings at those schools where they are wanting, especially at Peters Rest and Diamond ; the salaries to the female teachers may then be reduced. He further observed, that the female teachers at Peters Rest and La Princesse, whose attendance is actually required during all the hours of instruction, have applied to him for some additional payment to cover the expense of conveyance to the schools, he therefore urgently recommended to grant them until further $2 each pr. month. Council resolved to adopt the proposals of the Inspector, nominated its members Sarauw, Elliott and Arnesen to confer with Mr. Gardin concerning the cost attending the Erection of the two dwellings for teachers, and to make their proposals on the matter, also granted the increase proposed by the Inspector ; the needful report will be made to the Government.

Dear Sir ! þÿ There has been on several occasions a good deal of talk about public opinion or rather the want of public opinion and public spirit in this country, and it is very true, that even the facilities and encouragements held out by Government to the inhabitants for making their wants and wishes known have been responded to both here and at St. Thomas with unmistakable lukewarmness. But it is so natural for civilised man to take an interest not merely in what concerns him immediately, but also in matters that he knows will by their consequences affect his well-being, that much stronger evidence than that furnished by t:,e little experience we have hitherto had would be required to justify a conclusion so little flattering to the community as the one alluded to. The whole imputation arises in reality from a misconception of the circumstances. In a little community, in which owing to a preceding state of slavery, foreign birth, difference of nationality and other causes, unanimity and still in ro public spirit has been unknown, it is unreasonable to expect that the first symptoms of a rising public spirit should be evinced on abstract questions of representative government, liberty of the press etc. You might as well expect a child to understand the rules of grammar before it has become familiar with the use of its mother-tongue. From the London Times, Oct. I.) FRANCE. It is reported here that, in consequence of recent persecutions of Europeans in Madagascar, a combined English and French expedition against the Queen of this try is not improbable. Although that coun- would doubtless be a matter of no great difficulty in a military point of view, the dangerous climate, which in many parts of the island is almost inevitably fatal to Europeans, should suffice to deter from such an undertaking, unless it be deemed absolutely necessary. It is doubtless in a great measure owing to the climate that no permanent European settlements have been formed in Madagascar. The French had some mercantile establishments there for more than a century, but the Hungarian adventurer Beniowski, having endeavoured to render himself independent of France, in whose service he had gone to Madagascar, was attacked by the French themselves, killed, and the "establishment broken up. After 1815 the French again occupied two or three points of the island, butabaudoned them in IS31, after a disastrous war with the Ovas, one of the most powerful of the Madagascar tribes.

(From the Weekly Despatch, t PORTUGAL. Yellow fever had broken out at Lisbon. The weather was dry and sultry there. The quarantine laws are to be put in force. The Pope has assented to the concordat passed by the Cortes last session. The new Austrian Ambassador was expected at Lisbon shortly. M. Vasconcellos was likely to be the Minister of Justice; arid the electric telegraph wire is to terminate in Algarve. The inhabitants of Oporto have protested against the railway to Vigo, as calculated to drive Portuguese trade into Spain. PRUSSIA. The Evangelical Alliance held its last sitting on Friday evening. The meeting was attended by the King. On this occasion a Protestant pastor from Hungary depicted, in vigorous language, the obstructions thrown in the way of his co-religionists by the Austrian Government, and called upon the Alliance not to lose sight of this, not only in their prayers, but in their recommendations to their respective Governments. The Austrian envoy, being informed probably of the pastor's intention; to address the assembly, listened with evident symptoms of displeasure. Nor did be fail to take notes, doubtless, of all these, passages, which he may report, as hostile to the faith, if not to the administration of his Government. As a contrast to this, a Livonian (Russian) clergyman, lauded the subjects by liberty of conscience accorded were the Czar. rance.
